speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under Standing Order 41(2) I should like to lay on the table copies in both official languages of a document entitled "Mineral Policy Objectives for Canada".
A number of meetings have been held between the ministers responsible at the federal and provincial levels for mineral policy, culminating in a meeting in Ottawa on April 13 at which two decisions were concluded with respect to mineral policy in Canada.
The first of these has been the decision to set up a formal consultative and co-ordination mechanism in order to achieve more effective co-ordination in mineral policy development. Such a mechanism is essential for the formulation of mineral policies which are national in scope.
While noting that differences among governments on mineral policy matters remain, the ministers agreed that the real significance of their discussions is the beginning of new relationships among governments in the formulation of mineral policy for Canadians.
The meeting also reached agreement on the publication of a document entitled "Mineral Policy Objectives for Canada", which I am tabling today.
The document contains a more detailed description of the goal and objectives for mineral policies outlined in April, and is intended to form a background for further discussions by ministers. While this document relates to most minerals, it does not apply to fossil fuels. These, along with other energy commodities, will be the subject of extensive scrutiny within the context of papers reviewing Canada's energy policies which I will present to parliament in the near future.
Within the context of closer co-operation which is sought at the governmental level, governments must take into account each other's jurisdiction in the translation of objectives into policies. The document is not intended to state or identify policies by which any government would achieve such objectives, nor does it attempt to define or specify the particular role of any one government. However, it is a first phase in the process of intergovernmental co-operation for arriving at a mineral policy for Canada. None the less, governments will choose from a wide variety of strategies, programs, methods and techniques to achieve their objectives. References in the document tabled to possible strategies are therefore included only by way of example.
The publication of this document should be seen as a first step toward the formulation and implementation of comprehensive mineral policies for Canada.
The nation's mineral endowment can support an expanding level of output and thereby continue to contribute substantially to the economic and material well-being of future generations.
However, Canada does not have a monopoly on minerals. Indeed, Canada faces major challenges to maintain an internationally competitive sector because of increasing competition from other resource-producing nations and the efforts of larger industrial nations to secure greater long-term advantage from resource exporters.
Ministers want to explore how mineral development for both domestic needs and exports can be best undertaken to optimize long-term contribution to development throughout Canada. Such development must be sensitive to long-term economic needs, undesirable environmental impacts, the viability of communities dependent on mineral production and fabrication and more precise delineation of the long-term economic potential of our mineral endowment and the ways it can be utilized.

Mineral Policy Objectives
I urge Canadians interested in our resource development to study the contents of this document as the basis for informed discussion of those policies which will govern the important mineral sector of our economy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a statement on motions and table documents in both official languages under Standing Order 41(2).

On October 8, 1971, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) recognized the importance of the Canadian heritage by announcing the government policy on multiculturalism.
On that occasion, he said, and I quote:
... a policy of multiculturalism within a bilingual framework is basically the conscious support of individual freedom of choice. We are free to be ourselves. But this cannot be left to chance. It must be fostered and pursued actively. If freedom of choice is in danger for some ethnic groups, it is in danger for all. It is the policy of this government to eliminate any such danger and to "safeguard" this freedom.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian culture and identity are the fruit of diversity. Our literature, our art, our music, owe their wealth to that cultural heritage which we accept and develop.
Multiculturalism
Through our multiculturalism programs, we encourage an awareness of the cultural diversity that is characteristic of the Canadian society, while giving birth to a feeling of pride. We encourage Canadians, as groups and as individuals, to respect their own identity within the large Canadian family.
As Minister of State in charge of multiculturalism, I am happy to announce the expansion in some cases, and the implementation in others, of seven important programs whose purpose is to encourage the multicultural activities of Canadians.

There is an urgent need to establish a continuing and active communication with our ethno-cultural groups. To meet this need I would like to announce the formation of the Canadian Consultative Council on Multiculturalism. This council is representative of Canadians from every region of the country, and it is with pleasure that I table the terms of reference and the list of the first appointments today in both official languages according to Standing Order 41(2).
The new multicultural programs will entail an increase from the 1973-74 level of about $4 million to over $10 million. These increased funds for expanded and new programs reflect the government's commitment to the concept of multiculturalism.
As a first step we are enlarging the multicultural grants program which is the cornerstone of our policy of creating an awareness of Canada's multicultural diversity. Through this program, implemented in January, 1972, more than 300 ethno-cultural groups have received grants to undertake cultural and social projects. The response to this program has exceeded our expectations, and so a further $1,100,000 will be added to the budgetary estimates of this fiscal year to enable a greater number of groups to receive assistance for a wider variety of projects.
The second program expansion involves an increased allocation of funds from $154,000 to $654,000 during 1973-74 for the multicultural centres program. Grants have been made to such centres during the past year, and there are an additional 20 under way. These centres provide a vehicle for intercultural understanding throughout the country.
We are establishing a Canadian identities program. This is a major innovation designed to increase an awareness on the part of all Canadians of the cultural richness within our society. Expenditures under the Canadian identities program will be $3,823,500 in this fiscal year, of which $2,314,000 is already included in the estimates.
Assistance will be given to projects in the areas of films, radio and television broadcasting, folk festivals, theatre, literature, ethnic crafts and cuisine, travelling exhibits sponsored by the National Museum of Man, and the collection and exhibit programs of the Public Archives. A further $425,000 is provided for a multicultural studies program to encourage research in ethnic studies.
The ethnic press has a unique and very special role in Canadian life as a forum of discussion of community activities, and in many cases as the sole source of informa-

Multiculturalism
tion for many recent and elderly immigrants. The government will make greater use of the ethnic press this year to supply these various multicultural groups with helpful information on such things as pensions, immigration regulations, consumer protection, labour regulations, and National Housing Act provisions among other items.
The government will call its first national multicultural conference of ethno-cultural groups this fall with the assistance of the new Canadian Consultative Council on Multiculturalism.
To help young Canadians learn and retain their ancestral languages the federal government, in consultation with the provinces, has undertaken to provide language teaching aids. Some provinces and ethnic groups have expressed a concern that such aids are now available only from non-Canadian sources and are not sufficiently oriented to our nation's experience. Research on the role of ancestral languages in the retention of a culture is currently under way. This will be extended to include more groups and rural areas. However, the need for Canadian teaching material is already quite evident, and funds have been allocated for the provision of these teaching aids in 1973-74.
In dedicating ourselves to these innovative programs we are doing so convinced that cultural diversity is a positive asset to society. We are helping to provide a climate in which immigrants can immediately enter the mainstream of Canadian life, a climate in which young people can grow with a better understanding of and pride in their ethnic origins, a climate in which all ethno-cultural groups can develop. This policy leads to greater appreciation of the contributions that all our ethno-cultural groups are making to our national identity and, through this appreciation, to a greater appreciation and love for the colourful diversity so unique to our country.

speechtext:
The minister patted himself on the back very vigorously today, as on previous occasions, in an effort to create the impression it was he and the govern-

ment who invented the idea of multiculturalism in this country. I point out that in 1969, when the languages bill was before the committee and before the House, this party put forward amendments that clearly outlined our support of the principle of multiculturalism and our desire to do something positive to promote the idea.
In October, 1971, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced that the government had officially accepted the policy of multiculturalism. Of course we welcomed that announcement and I welcome the steps being taken today to promote the concept of multiculturalism. I think we all agree there is a positive value in the contribution made to the Canadian cultural fabric by groups other than the two official language groups. As a matter of fact, if we are concerned about maintaining an identity for this country different from that of the country south of the border, our only hope may lie in preserving and encouraging the growth of these various cultures within our own borders.
I was very disappointed at the lack of an explanation in the minister's statement of how the policy will be implemented. No provision is being made for the consultative council to have a real input into the policy-making process in regard to multiculturalism. As I interpret the document, the policy will be handed down from on high and the function of the council will be to advise the government on how to implement it. I think that is approaching the problem from the wrong direction; there has to be an input from the ethnic groups themselves in the area of policy development as well as in the implementation of policy.
I am somewhat concerned about the method used to select members of the consultative council. From my travels across the country and discussions with representatives of the various ethnic groups I know that there has been virtually no or very little consultation with them on how the members of the council should be selected, and certainly there was no opportunity for ethnic groups to elect members to this council. The appointments were made by the minister. I am not making accusations of any kind, but it does leave the whole thing in question because of the lack of democracy in the way the council was set up.
I was also extremely distressed that no reference was made to changes in the policies regarding the mass media, particularly the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. This applies particularly to the present policy of television and radio stations prohibiting the use of third languages.
If we are serious about promoting the concept of multiculturalism and sensitizing the Canadian public to the concept so that it can be fully understood and therefore more fully implemented, it is obvious we have to use all means at our disposal to make this sensitization possible. It seems to me that use of the mass media is the obvious choice. No reference whatsoever has been made to this, and I am very disappointed.
On the positive side, I am pleased to see efforts are being made to provide teaching aids in an attempt to provide a greater degree of third language education. I think that is a very useful step. I should like to see some change in the teaching of Canadian history in schools. At present, due credit is not given to the third force and its contribution to the development of this country. I think the history books
May 17, 1973

being used in our schools are defective and need to be improved.
If I may touch the conscience of the National Film Board a little, I hope the minister will ensure more open consultation with ethnic groups involved when films are being made about them. There have been examples of films produced in the past when consultations with the particular group about which the film was made were not held, with the result that the films produced were found to be repugnant to the particular groups concerned. I think that is a shameful situation and should not be allowed to recur under any circumstances.
I should like to comment also on the communications portion of the minister's statement. It is indicated that the government will purchase space in various newspapers to publish details of various events and programs in which the government is participating. I think there is a better way of doing this than simply by buying space in this way. I think we could go much further than that in the provision of news to the ethnic press. I suggest that an ethnic press service bureau be established, funded by the department, which would be staffed with a press gallery member whose function it would be to gather news for the ethnic press of this country. The staff associated with him would make this news presentable in such a form that it could be used by the ethnic press.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I want to chastise the minister for having recently engaged in a massive propaganda campaign promoting himself, the Prime Minister and his party.

Mr. Speaker, the announcement that the government is prepared to increase the support it will give to the various ethnic communities in this country will, I am certain, be supported by all parties and by all members in the House. In making his statement the minister reminded us that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) first made an announcement about this matter in October of 1971. There has been much too long a period between the announcement by the Prime Minister and any implementation.
We are not now dealing with the kind of situation the government had to face at the beginning of the LIP or OFY program when organizations had to be established. The ethnic organizations are alive and well and flourishing in all parts of Canada. Until now, however, there has been very little action, and I want to say to the minister that I consider what we have had until now as nothing but the worst kind of tokenism. There is no reason why it took until now to announce that the government was prepared to spend the money that the minister announced today. The ethnic organizations could have spent, from the beginning, ten times what the government has announced it is prepared to put into the program today. This program should have started a year and a half or more ago.
I am disturbed by the fact that, certainly as of several weeks ago, there had been no meaningful discussions with the provinces. A number of provinces have already begun implementing programs to support ethnic organizations in the fields of language, music, dancing and art. It seems to me ridiculous that there is a distinct possibility of duplication of the work being funded by the provinces and that being funded by the federal government. I cannot understand why there has not been not only discussion in a formal way but the closest kind of consultation in planning so that federal and provincial programs would fit together rather than being developed in completely separate ways.
The last point I want to make is that I am not satisfied with the way in which, until now, programs chosen to be funded have been picked. So far as I can find out there have been no real, meaningful consultations with the various ethnic communities. The criteria under which these programs have been funded until now have not been adequately explained to those communities in such a way that they can understand why some ethnic groups have had projects financed while others that seemed to be equally deserving have been passed over. They have been told they have been passed over without being told when or if they will be getting funds.
If the announcement today by the minister that the consultative committee has been chosen means that there will be real liaison between the government department, which in my view until now has been choosing projects at best in a very bureaucratic fashion, and the ethnic communities and the people they represent, if the committee will in fact form a bridge between the government and the ethnic communities, then a real step forward will have been taken. If not, I predict that the minister will be hearing an increasing volume of criticism about the way in which the government has until now been choosing projects.

Today, this same very idealistic Canadian, Rene Levesque, leads the Parti Quebecois, pledged to separatism from this type of government. There is your unity, aspirations and operations of this government. That is my first comment.
The next point I want to deal with is taxation. I have only glanced through these documents, but I could not find any mention of the main curse of the mining industry in Canada, I refer to the taxation system of the provinces and the taxation system of the federal government. I say flatly to the minister and the whole of this country that the Benson tax reforms will destroy every Canadian mining company, the small companies within 10 years and the big integrated companies within 30 years when the mines run out. Unless these taxation laws are changed, there will be no future for the Canadian mining industry. It will go down the drain as surely as the Canadian oil and gas industry went down the drain in the past 20 years because of the taxation policies of the federal government and the type of policies adopted by the provincial governments.
With regard to the provinces, I wish to mention one thing only. I think this will interest the leader of the New Democratic Party. One of the things the provinces have done with regard to both oil and gas and mining, and the federal government is no better, is to front-end load these resource industries so much by all the charges they could put together with their fertile minds. Thus they have added to the capital cost of these very precarious operations, so much so that in Canada today the main cost of mining is the cost of money because of the huge debts owed not only to the lenders but to the provincial and federal government. As far I can see, this is not mentioned in this booklet, but this evil of front-end loading, which will lead to most of the oil, gas and minerals being left in the ground, must be stopped by every government, not just the federal government. We would like to see the minister make a clear statement on these matters in order to make the mining industry what it could be to Canada.
The preamble makes it very clear that there is a great future for Canada. The future of our nation depends on the wise use of our oil, gas and energy resources. It depends on the wise use of our mineral resources. I wish to
May 17, 1973

give an example of what I am talking about. By reason of improper handling of its energy resources, our great neighbour to the south will have a deficit in its international balance of payments by the year 1975, or 1980 at the latest, of $30 billion a year for energy alone because they did not take the proper steps in time. Even though minerals are not a part of their current crisis, by the end of this century, for every dollar that the Americans are short in balance of payments because of a shortage of energy they will be $2 short on minerals. Their estimated deficit in international payments by the end of this century will be $60 billion a year. With this great problem facing our neighbour to the south, it is absolutely imperative we have a government in power that will move in the direction ensuring that these resources are used to the maximum advantage not only of this country but of the whole world.
I hold to the view that a lot of plain speaking has to be done in connection with the mining industry. If we want to share in greater returns from this industry, we have to stop this front-end loading and allow higher returns so the companies can pay off their debts. Under the oil regulations in the north the provinces grabbed all they could in the first year, front-end loaded the industry and were satisfied with 121/2 per cent interest. In 1961 under the federal regulations for the north it took an average of 60 per cent to get them into a cash flow position. We can do the same thing with mines if we plan properly. The key is taxation.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, these ten years of inaction with no mineral policy and no energy policy have cost this country dearly. We have seen our gas and oil industry become foreign owned as a result of Canadian taxation. We are seeing the mining industry go the same way. All other industries will follow unless we face the fact that taxation today plays a part in international competition. If the provinces and the federal government continue to have no awareness that our tax policies must become competitive, not in order to get less money from the industry but to give more money to the people, then the future of this country is-no future. I suggest that the repentance I see in this statement today comes too late, about ten years too late. If only the government had followed the course that we set between 1959 and 1961 we would not be in this mess today complaining about the lack of Canadian ownership.

Mr. Speaker, it is regrettable that the minister's statement went astray. Apparently it was put in the mails and some people have very optimistic ideas about the speed of the mails in this country. The next time the minister wants to put a statement in the mail, I suggest that he make his speech one week later, which is about the length of time it takes to send anything through the mails.
The decision of the federal and provincial governments to set up a co-ordinating mechanism for consultation and co-operation with respect to objectives in developing the mineral resources of this country is, of course, a good one. But when I read the minister's statement and glance at the material that has been put before us, I cannot help feeling that this government is falling into the trap it falls into again and again. Whenever the machine begins to slow
Mineral Policy Objectives
down, the government adds another wheel, another pulley, instead of adding to the power that drives the machine. All that happens is that the machine slows down even more.
Of course the provinces need a mechanism for consultation and co-operation, and I support the proposal that the minister is now putting forward. But they also need something much more fundamental: they need a national minerals policy, and they have not had a national minerals policy. You cannot make up for lack of leadership merely by setting up another committee or consultative body, which is what the government is trying to do.
I agree with the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) that this country needs a national minerals policy. I do not agree with him that what we need to do is to reduce the taxes on mining companies further. I cannot shed tears over International Nickel Company which has been making hundreds of millions of dollars out of resources that belong to the people of Canada.
The spokesman for the Progressive Conservative party talks about the poor oil and gas companies going down the drain during the last ten years. Imperial Oil, after taxes, made $1 billion during the last 20 years and has paid to the government of Canada royalties of $40 million, or 4 per cent of what they pocketed for themselves from the resources of Canada.

The federal government has control over the export of these materials since they grant the export permits. I am not suggesting that this can be done in 24 hours, but I am suggesting that the provinces and the mining industry can be told that exports of raw minerals will be phased out over a period of years and that they must be processed in this country. This would create jobs, give a greater tax return and improve economic development for the people of Canada.
The second thrust must be for the federal government- the provinces cannot do this-to join with other mineral producing countries in order to negotiate better prices from the importing countries. Raw materials in the past have had a relatively low return in comparison with manufactured goods which countries like Canada have to buy back. The only way this can be done is for Canada to join with other mineral producing countries and negotiate reasonable prices so that we will get a better return for the people of Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT TAKE MEASURES TO SAFEGUARD RIGHTS OF FRANCOPHONE AND ANGLOPHONE CANADIANS
speechtext:
That this House deplores the government's decision to postpone the full implementation of the policy contained in the Official Languages Act and censures the solutions proposed by the government, and consequently, urges the latter to find realistic and specific ways of safeguarding the rights of French- and Englishspeaking Canadians in a much more just and reasonable manner.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I particularly thank you for correcting the error contained in the text of the motion.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is high time in Canada as well as in this House that we clarify a certain situation, because for much too long the government of this country-more particularly the administration-has only put up a bilin-

gual front while we all very well know that we are governed by an exclusively English-speaking establishment.
Mr. Speaker, not to admit that this situation exists is not to be aware of what is happening. For about five years, I have had the honour to represent the Champlain riding in the House and during this period I could notice that the administrative services, as soon as it comes to an important level, do not have any French-speaking person, apart from a number of assistants who are there to help indirectly or in a parallel way but not so as to allow French Canadians to really feel at home here and within the government.
Mr. Speaker, it is urgent that not only the appearance of this country be bilingual but it is also important that the structures and members of administration and management be actually distributed according to a just and fair proportion of the ethnic components in our society. For a long time now we have been living in hope. After the passage of the Official Languages Act in 1969, great expectation arose because we felt that at least we held the key to French Canada's problem.
Mr. Speaker, that great expectation was expressed in the preamble to the motion proposed by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) last April 13. The preamble reads as follows and I quote:
(i) aware that, as provided in the Official Languages Act, the English and French languages possess and enjoy equality of status and equal rights and privileges as to their use in all the institutions of the Parliament and Government of Canada;
cognizant that it is the duty of departments and agencies of the Government of Canada to ensure, in accordance with that Act, that members of the public can obtain available services from and communicate with them in both official languages; while
recognizing that public servants should, as a general proposition and subject to the requirements of the Official Languages Act respecting the provision of services to the public, be able to carry out their duties in the Public Service of Canada in the official language of their choice;
Mr. Speaker, we fully agree with that preamble. We would like to see those principles become reality. We all agree on that point but we disagree when the time comes to apply these principles. Since the inception of the law we must say, Mr. Speaker, that not only did we not progress but, according to statistics, we are at a standstill and even rolling backwards in some areas.
On behalf of our party, on behalf of the official French Canadian opposition since our party has 15 out of 16 French-speaking members, we must say in this House what French Canada or, more precisely, what Quebec wants. This is why we believe that it was urgent to introduce a motion dealing with that problem even though the Prime Minister had already introduced a motion. The motion is an attempt to create an objective and realistic atmosphere, an atmosphere free of any emotion, animosity and struggle which might even remotely be interpreted as a racial struggle. No, Mr. Speaker. We are quite fair and we would like, especially on this special day, to see French-Canadian members better represented, especially those of the Liberal party, since I can see only three or four members from the Liberal party, which thinks of itself as the defender of bilingualism and biculturalism par excellence.
Official Languages
We have thus, Mr. Speaker, to concur that we are agreed on the principles on bilingualism contained in the Official Languages Act, and also on the motion introduced by the right hon. Prime Minister, that we have also to admit that we are greatly disappointed by the tangible means by which, supposedly, justice is to be done once and for all. I wish therefore, in my speech, to deal first with the Canadian history aspect, then with the present situation and, finally, to suggest our very tangible solutions.
It must be admitted that French Canadians have been deprived of their rights, ever since they were conquered, obviously, but more especially since 1867. I will not speak of their privileges, because they never had any. That is historical fact. We have been continually forced to carry on "extremist" fights to obtain rights that were sometimes as basic as that of speaking and being answered in our mother tongue.
It will be remembered, Mr. Speaker, that there were epic struggles to obtain bilingual cheques, bilingual money, bilingual stamps and a distinctive flag. Mr. Speaker, all these struggles should normally have been enough to permanently discourage the French Canadians, but their courage and tenacity have been such that they have overcome all these obstacles; unfortunately, however, the governments that succeeded one another always believed it was sufficient for the French Canadians to be satisfied and content to state principles and they believed they could solve all problems with a French Canadian party leader or Prime Minister. That was sufficient. The mere fact that the great Sir Wilfrid Laurier's name was Laurier, that he was a French Canadian, was sufficient to prevent all French Canadians from recriminating and demanding. The mere presence of a man at the head of the government was enough to satisfy the French Canadians who were then submerged in a period of darkness and were almost all non educated.
Later on, they realized that it took more than that but again the grand and great Liberal party solved the problem by electing Mr. Louis Stephen St-Laurent who, besides being a French Canadian prime minister, advocated good understanding for years. Again that seemed to satisfy the French Canadians since they were then at the dawn of a period of emancipation.
They seemed to be satisfied when the Liberal party was supported wholeheartedly with the Right Hon. Louis St-Laurent. Finally, people came to realize over the last few years that this was not sufficient and then we found a miracle solution with the coming of the Messiah, the current Prime Minister. Now, the Prime Minister is no longer content with having a French Canadian name nor with preaching good-will; he goes, I admit, a bit further. He incorporated into a law the principles that where only spoken about at the time of the hon. Louis St-Laurent and that were hardly mentioned at all at the time of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Those principles were put in writing in 1968 and particularly in 1969 by the adoption of the Official Languages Act.
The proof is now established, as this happened four years afeo, that no change occurred. This is why it is our duty, as the French-Canadian official opposition in this

May 17, 1973
Official Languages
House, to state things as they are, to point out the trouble and all together, I am convinced, with everybody's goodwill, we shall reach true solutions because, as you know, the Quebecer or the French Canadian has changed in that today he will not be content with principles. In fact, a fair proportion of Quebecers are disillusioned vis-a-vis the federal policy and with regards to how they are received by public servants and particularly by top administrators, we must agree that they are right and this is one of the reasons which have lead-I have had the opportunity to witness that on the front benches, for instance-the hon. Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier), his colleague, the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) and the right hon. Prime Minister himself to show Quebec that it was possible for French Canadians to have their share and obtain in the administration of this country the position they deserve. I do not know whether those three ministers, that used to be called the three doves, are also disillusioned but I have had the opportunity, at the beginning of this session, of hearing not only the Prime Minister but also the Minister of Transport deliver speeches, right here in the House. The latter expressed more or less what I am now saying, disappointment, going so far as to say that he was prepared to drop everything and leave if there were no change.
Now, Mr. Speaker, all we want to do is help the government settle the problem once and for all. This is not the time, when there is so much agitation in Quebec, with the situation critical, when it can truly be said that there is a real problem. It is not when a good proportion of Quebecers want French unilingualism in Quebec that we should come forward with such timid policy statements. I feel that would be showing complete lack of objectivity and realism. Let us be realistic. Let us not, practicing the policy of the ostrich, believe that in 1973 we can solve our problems by policy statements.
Mr. Speaker, the very future of our country rests particularly in the hands of French Canada. I am not saying so to brag, to push one ethnic origin rather than another, but it is well known throughout the country that if there were no French Canada, there just would not be a Canada at all and that if Canada does exist, if we are an entity different from the American entity, it is because there is a Quebec, because there are French Canadians. And therefore, our hon. colleagues from all Canadian provinces, more particularly from the west, and from Ontario, should not only give more concrete acceptance to the French fact in our country, but even more heaven and earth, in favour of great progress in Canada, not only to protect the interests of French Canadians, but also those of all other Canadians.
I think this aspect is important, Mr. Speaker, for however much we talk about unity and harmony, there is no escaping the fact that we must also talk about the facts, and there can only be harmony or unity if there is agreement between Canadians of different origin. So let us not take it for granted that Canadians of French origin are today not ready to co-operate to the full for the emancipation and fulfilment of Canada. We would like to build up a national consciousness in this country, we would like to feel here that we are really true Canadians, but for this to happen, all of us, in all the provinces from coast to coast,

have great need of the French-speaking cultural contribution and French-Canadian participation.
Mr. Speaker, this picture of our present situation leads me to think that there have always been difficulties in implementing principles, even the Constitution. Reading the sections of the British North America Act that deal with the rights of the French language in this country, we still find them ambiguous and a source of renewed disputes and problems. Therefore, if this document is not sufficiently clear, it must be changed. And if at some point we find ourselves under the yoke called Confederation, why should we not be able to change this wretched yoke, if that is what is preventing harmony and unity in Canada.
And so, since certain sections of the Constitution are not clear enough regarding linguistic sharing and rights, we should simply think of changing them. Of course, you could answer that the Official Languages Act is supposed to do just that, and that there is no need to amend the Constitution, but then, although the principles of this act are extremely fair, and were adopted by all Members of Parliament in 1969, what has happened since then? We have seen people raise obstacles, people from the establishment try by all means to impede the implementation of the Official Languages Act. Who were those people? We do not know. It seems that in the establishment of high officials it is very difficult to know those things. But in any case some Members of Parliament reacted and I would like to point out a statement made not by anybody but by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) who said yesterday, and I quote:
It would be racial discrimination to want to set up special programs to recruit French-speaking people in the public service.
When we want to implement principles the Leader of the Opposition himself, undoubtedly under pressure from different parts of the country, objects to increasing the participation of French-speaking people in the administration simply to make an abnormal thing normal. But since the country has been in an abnormal situation for years, the suggestion of coming back to a normal situation seems revolutionary because we have grown accustomed to a routine, we have become encrusted and we imagine that when French Canadians demand equality in this country that cannot be done-

Mr. He ward Grafftey (Brome-Missisquoi): I simply want to point out immediately that the Leader of the Opposition did not make any such statement and everybody knows that. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT TAKE MEASURES TO SAFEGUARD RIGHTS OF FRANCOPHONE AND ANGLOPHONE CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will merely point out to the hon. member that I was reading a text that I have in my hand and the contents of which he may check himself.
Anyhow, Mr. Speaker, the principles must be unanimously approved by the House. We realize that when they are to be implemented, several put a spoke in the wheels.
May 17, 1973

During the last electoral campaign, there were unfortunately some candidates in several constituencies who took advantage of that situation to get elected. It is not funny, but that is what happened.
Now, Mr. Speaker, such a thing should not happen again. We should not, in order to keep up appearances and soothe the feelings of the various ethnic groups in this country, say that we are in favour. We are all in favour of bilingualism, we want French-Canadians to obtain justice, but we merely agree and remain idle. However, it is too late now, we have reached a much further stage, hence the need for the motion which we are introducing today.
Mr. Speaker, I should also mention that when I speak as I now do, I have major reasons to do so, and roughly I should say that the Commissioner of Official Languages, appointed as a result of the adoption of the legislation, recognizes and deplores the situation, and those who attended meetings of the Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates and heard Mr. Spicer's evidence were able to see that he made no bones about saying he was disappointed and even disillusioned and that in his opinion things were not going as they should.
Mr. Spicer went so far as to say that the deadline, as far as he is concerned, is not 1978 as planned by the government, but that we have a mere two years from now to achieve the objectives of the Official Languages Act.
Mr. Speaker, when the bilingualism ombudsman, Mr. Spicer, reaches the same conclusions as we do, taking into consideration complaints received and analyses and studies carried out, I do not believe hon. members in this House can doubt his word.
Mr. Speaker, I repeat that it is time to act. Words we have heard and no doubt will hear again, but we need action. I refer to the speech that the Right Hon. Prime Minister, Mr. Pearson, made April 6, 1966:
To this end, and having regard to the character of our country, the government for several years has been taking practical steps to encourage bilingualism in the federal public service as part of its fundamental objective of promoting and strengthening national unity on the basis of the equality of rights and opportunities for both English speaking and French speaking Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, again, we all agree on this. That was in 1966, but we are now in 1973. What practical change has taken place? That is the problem. On September 28, 1963, Mr. Gilles Lalande said, and I quote:
-That the federal government, which has instructed the Lau-rendeau-Dunton Royal Commission in its terms of reference to make recommendations such as to ensure the bilingual and basically bicultural nature of the federal administration, not only encourage the sporadic use of French in Ottawa, but also allow French-Canadians to start working according to their own culture in certain units of the federal administration. Because it is important to put an end as soon as possible to the era of French Canadian deputy directors, isolated and lost in Anglo-Saxon surroundings, and to do away with the misleading practice of having representatives, French-speaking or with a French name, on boards of directors.
And Mr. Lalande, Mr. Speaker, is not a member of the Social Credit party, as far as I know, and to enlighten the House, I should say he was the co-secretary of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism. I go on quoting:
The wrong solution: Bilingualism.
Official Languages
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, the problem in this country is not one of languages. The problem in this country is a problem of participation and even if the entire federal administration were bilingual, if 90 or 95 per cent of the administrators are English-speaking, nothing would be solved since the French Canadian would not yet feel at home. Thus, it is wrong to solve the problem by bilingualism.
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the point of view of westerners, for intance, when they do not see the necessity of learning French to climb the administrative ladder. I understand them, I approve them; they are right because it is not a problem of languages and we must not ignore people who are really competent on the grounds that they do not know another language. Mr. Speaker, as far as I know, American people with their scientists succeeded in launching satellites in space and they did it in English. We all know as well that the Russian people did it and they did so in Russian. Competence, in any area, is not a matter of language and the world has known geniuses who worked in all languages. I think it is stupid to require that someone know another language to give him a position. It is stupid and those who criticize this point of view are right.
Areas where bilingualism becomes a factor of competence, since it can be in some areas, are of minor significance. It would be rather inappropriate, for instance, to hire a unilingual guide or security agent for the central door of the Parliament building. It would be inappropriate to hire a unilingual stewardess, train engineer, telephone operator or receptionist. At that level bilingualism becomes a factor of competence, but not at other levels.
Therefore, to find the true solution we need parallel administration where anyone, be he French- or Englishspeaking, will have access to all administrative positions including that of deputy minister. This is the solution. This is the solution we were advocating during the last election campaign and it is clearly established. We know that the solution has already been "preached" in 1963 by none other than the co-secretary of the Laurendeau-Dun-ton commission and this is why these recommendations are ours today because we know that this is the only solution. We will never be able to impose bilingualism to people-who are not interested in it and I understand them-under the pretense that we want to introduce this concept here. This is a false solution and, Mr. Speaker, I see that you are about to rise to remind me that my time is expired-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not abuse my colleagues' kindness but I think it is important that the government should adopt the solution we are advocating. We have no exclusive rights to it.

May 17, 1973
Official Languages
All the less as some people thought about it. So Mr. Lalande said, and I quote:
Nothing would be more untrue and indeed more detrimental to the national interests of French Canada than to seek that basically bicultural character in Canadian institutions above all through bilingualism.
The French Canadians could not settle their participation problem through bilingualism.
Nothing would be more dangerous for the French Canadians than to let the pursuing of a cultural interpretation by the French speaking and English speaking elements in the federal public service or to sit and watch a generalization of the half-English half-French formula already advocated by certain ministers lacking in inspiration. Of course, steps must be taken to spread the knowledge of the French and English languages among the staff of the federal public service serving bilingual people, as it is done in big private business. But where decisions are in the making, where policies, the impact of which will affect the country as a whole, are worked out (in federal departments or within the federal bureaucracy in Ottawa), the administration could never replace bicultural management however imperfect it may be, by purely bilingual elements, should they even be partly French Canadians.
Mr. Chairman, this is the solution. French Canadians must feel completely at home in Ottawa; they must participate and to enable him to do so, executive positions must be opened to him where the rights and privileges of no one will be infringed upon. This is the reason why by setting up separate French and English units within all departments, we will be able to create an equality for which all French Canadians long so much, but not a mathematical or numerical equality but one based on needs. It should be understood, for instance, that obviously, the French network of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation does not have the same scope as the English network because its needs are not as great. The French network of the CBC does not need so many television or radio stations as the English network. This is quite normal, but there is an equality and, as far as I know, nobody has ever criticized the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in this regard and complained that there is only one corporation but two independent networks, though they work along together very well within one corporation.
I go on quoting the statement by Mr. Lalande:
As for us, we are of the opinion that real biculturalism demands at least in part the duality of agencies ... To refuse systematically the formula of duality is as far as we are concerned, to show preference for the maintenance of a bicultural front; it also means to believe in a myth, namely "national culturalism". But to accept to consider it, on the contrary, means not to refuse to entertain in a concrete manner the seeping of French-Canadian vigour into the concepts and methods that are far too English prevailing in all our so-called Canadian institutions; finally, it means being ready to live a true biculturalism.
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to quote those comments made by the secretary of the Laurendeau-Dunton Commission because they agree with our own program. I am sure that even if we persist in trying to implement a complete, awkward and costly sort of bilingualism and quote figures, and even if the government were to order an enquiry into the matter, people would realized that the type of federal administration we advocate would be less costly than the extensive bilingualism that we are now seeking to implement. In fact, although French is being taught to

unilingual English-speaking civil servants, will that change anything? Through what miracle will these people transmit their knowledge to those who will come after them?
So, there is no alternative but to give each and every citizen a chance for true emancipation and fulfilment and thus we will achieve, and we French Canadians will be glad to co-operate participation, in building a truly Canadian nation. We shall then be able to work together toward the betterment of our population as a whole.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to say as briefly as possible that this afternoon I intend to discuss bilingualism not as a member of the Progressive Conservative party, which would be quite natural, as I am a member of that party-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT TAKE MEASURES TO SAFEGUARD RIGHTS OF FRANCOPHONE AND ANGLOPHONE CANADIANS
speechtext: We have nothing against that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT TAKE MEASURES TO SAFEGUARD RIGHTS OF FRANCOPHONE AND ANGLOPHONE CANADIANS
speechtext:
-but as a Canadian Member of Parliament. I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that if we do discuss bilingualism along party lines we will be waging an electoral battle here in this House and it is our country, Canada, that will suffer thereby.
I do not want to dwell too long on my leader's position but where bilingualism is concerned, I want to work as a Canadian in this House, along with the Social Credit members, the New Democratic Party members, the Liberal members and my own colleagues. But let us be realistic; you know as well as I do where my leader, the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) stands with regard to bilingualism.
I will say it again: if we are to discuss bilingualism and stick to our party lines, it is our country, Canada that will suffer, and this parliament might suffer too, Mr. Speaker.
As member for Brome-Missisquoi, I don't want to go into too many details, Mr. Speaker, but here in Ottawa, I have the honor-and one cannot imagine how proud I am of it-to represent a riding which is 95 per cent Frenchspeaking. Unfortunately, when I entered politics, in Ottawa, my French was awful. But today, I don't want to discuss the matter of length. The fact is that as a member representing Brome-Missisquoi in Ottawa, I have not been commissioned by my constituents to discuss bilingualism and official languages and make a political play of it. [English]
There will be some who will think I am talking in motherhood cliches, Mr. Speaker, when I say that I want to underline once and for all-I sometimes suspect politicians when they say outside of the economic arena that this thing or that thing must be discussed in a bipartisan approach-that I am convinced as I have never been convinced before that if we discuss language rights in a political arena such as this House of Commons, or back in our ridings or during an election campaign, it is this institution which suffers; it is Canada which suffers. The approach of our party has always been the same. When the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was Prime Minister-and I underline that I do not say this in a partisan way-we were prepared to take a bipartisan approach to constitutional modernization. We were prepared to take a bipartisan approach to language rights and
May 17, 1973

the question of whether or not they should be reenshrined in the constitution, as they always have been.
Let me say this. It was to be a modern constitution for modern times. Whether or not it involved the improvement of language rights in Ottawa, the right hon. gentleman told me, told the opposition of the day and told every member of his caucus that we must take a bipartisan approach to this issue. At that time Mr. Laurendeau very sincerely put forward the proposition of the B and B Commission. We did not reject it out of hand, but thought we had a better approach. It was at that time unfortunately-and I am not naming any members of any party-that certain individuals both inside and outside this House tried to paint our party as anti-Quebec. Nonsense. We had our way and others had their way.
[ Translation]
And unfortunately, since then, and too often indeed especially during the last decade, we have been discussing this business of official languages and bilingualism, within and without this House from political viewpoints.
Many times, Mr. Speaker-

If in the past I have rarely spoken on this subject, if in the past I have been shy about talking on this subject, it has been because my constituents do not really encourage me to do this. In the little village in which I live there are 500 families, 250 of which are French-speaking and 250 of which are English-speaking. My executive assistant here in Ottawa speaks French to his mother and English to his father. Do you think I have a mandate to discuss in a partisan way this issue which goes to the very fabric of the nation? No.

And I ask each member to take that question out of its political context as soon as possible in the best interests of the country.
Mr. Speaker, the Confederation Act enacted over a 100 years ago was an act of faith in which the Liberals and the Conservatives co-operated to lay the foundations of our country, Canada. The Fathers of Confederation discussed at the very beginning not from a political tribune or as Tories and Grits. They were first of all Canadians. It is therefore quite natural from time to time to deal with the matter as politicians, because the enticements were there. I admit that it was done before and after but in general, it can be said that the debates on Confederation were carried on outside the political field by the Fathers of Confederation.
It seems to me superfluous to say that the issue of official languages must be discussed in the same spirit. I wish to state that each member, either a New Democrat, a Creditiste, a Liberal or a Progressive Conservative, wants to discuss about the welfare of Canada before dealing with the welfare of his political party.
Today, however we do not only have the Liberals and the Progressive Conservatives, but also our friends the New Democrats and the Creditistes.
Official Languages
[ English!
But there is one more thing, Mr. Speaker, and let us put the cards on the table right away. If we were discussing the future of Canada as the Fathers of Confederation did 100 years ago, Liberals and Conservatives together putting Canada first, we would have to remember, whether we were discussing constitutional provisions or language rights, that Canada was a different country in those years. Toward the end of the last century, during the beginning of this century and even today, many people have been coming to this great land of ours to share in the experience of nation building, people who either call themselves Francophones or are from the United Kingdom. I am not just speaking of the west where the multicultural force is so great, but those people must certainly feel left out of this debate. It reminds me somewhat of charter members of an old club arguing over who comes first while the new members are left out. Let us stop this nonsense. We can stop it, especially with the makeup of the present House of Commons, if we let every iota of partisanship out of this debate.

Mr. Speaker, there is another thing that I want to discuss very clearly in a not too partisan manner, I hope. But I direct my remarks today especially to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) and occasionally to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet).
I deplore the fact, Mr. Speaker, that we are only two representatives from the province of Quebec in the Progressive Conservative party and I am sure that the Liberals are sorry they did not even elect one member from the province of Alberta. It may be unfortunate for national unity but when the ministers see that we are not a national party, can the Liberals honestly think that it is a good thing for national unity and the future of our country? The Liberal party is a great national party, and so is ours, and I do everything I can as a Progressive Conservative member from the province of Quebec to build efficiently the two-party system. And when the ministers see that we are not a national party, when they did not even win one seat in Alberta, they are playing with the fabric of our country, Canada. The Liberals are a national party, and so are we.
In 1958, when there were only 48 Liberals in Parliament and more than half were from the province of Quebec, not even once did we find that the Liberal party was not a national party, because it was indeed a national party. No one should say that. I talked on several occasions with my colleagues of the Liberal party from the province of Quebec and they regret as often as I do the statements made by the Postmaster General, the Minister of Transport and even the Prime Minister.

Let us nail that to the wall right away. There are two great national parties in this House.

speechtext:
I withdraw. You are right. There are four national parties in this House, whether or not we have

May 17, 1973
Official Languages
equal distribution. I stand corrected. The minute we start throwing rhetoric around-and we never did it in 1958 when over 50 per cent of the Liberal caucus was drawn from my province-it ceases to be a joking matter. Sometimes we say statesmanlike things here on the floor of the House only to appear on television back home in our ridings not always saying the same things. At the risk of repeating one cliche after another, I appeal to the House for the fourth or fifth time to stop that kind of nonsense and approach this subject in a bipartisan all-Canadian way.

In the province of Quebec-let us be realistic-the minister of Transport claims that the sole federalist party in Canada is the Liberal party. If this is really true, we, as Quebecers, at the federal and provincial levels, have only the choice between the Grits and Rene Levesque; the Parti quebecois will accede to power sooner than expected. Such a belief is ridiculous and I am a federalist even if I reject the kind of federalism or the federalist doctrine of the right hon. prime minister, that of confrontation. I do not accept it but I remain, I hope, as good a federalist as he is.
But when it is claimed that there is but one choice in Quebec, the Grits or the Parti quebecois, this is quite dangerous for national unity and everybody knows it as well as I do.

There is no such simple choice, and no demogoguery or simplistic argument will prove otherwise.

I definitely share, Mr. Speaker, the views stated today by the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte), as well as most of his ideas, but I am certain that as a Quebecer, I have often heard the speeches of the leader of the Social Credit party of Canada (Mr. Caouette) in Quebec. He is often right when he deals with economic questions; he wants bread and butter on the table of all our fellow-citizens. When the leader of the Social Credit party of Canada deals with economic questions, when he says in Quebec that our fellow-citizens must be in a position to support themselves, I agree. This is why we must not let an issue such as bilingualism be raised up in a political context in the House or at the next election.
Fifteen years ago, I was elected for the first time as member for Brome-Missisquoi. I was not satisfied as far as bilingualism was concerned. I was quite often compelled to return unilingual documents to bureaucrats to obtain a translation. But I did not need a Royal Commission of Inquiry on Bilingualism and Biculturalism to tell me that my secretary should be bilingual, because it is absolutely essential.
I wonder to what extent-the Creditiste leader has quite often spoken about that-the issue will be settled with some regulation or commission here and there. We would rather settle the matter in good faith and in a fine Canadian spirit. I hope that during the next weeks we will speak as united Canadians.
Naturally, Mr. Speaker, there are many issues, not necessarily economic, that we sometimes discuss, although perhaps we should not, in a very partisan way. It is my hope, however, that we will approach the next election fighting on bread and butter issues. There is not a member of this House of Commons, no matter where he comes from in Canada, who has been given a firm mandate by his constituents to let this issue get into the political arena. I believe that, as I have never believed anything before. That is the mandate, the very special mandate of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). It is the mandate of all of us. He knows where the Leader of the Opposition stands on this issue.
More than anything it is the duty of the Prime Minister to pull this issue out of the political partisan arena. Whether it is a resolution that is coming before us, whether it is a bill that is coming before us, let us be very careful about the consequences. Any time someone gets up to discuss a detail of that resolution or that bill he may be labelled anti this or anti that. There may be some shortterm gain, but there is only going to be long-term chaos.
If I have repeated myself perhaps seven or eight times I have done so because, while we do not talk about it in my riding and I do not think we talk about it all that much in Canada, it is a subject about which if we really believe in Canada and its future, we feel deeply. It is deep down in our dreams of national unity.

I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that we will tackle the issue of bilingualism during the next few weeks as Canadians rather than as members of political parties.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT TAKE MEASURES TO SAFEGUARD RIGHTS OF FRANCOPHONE AND ANGLOPHONE CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin my remarks this afternoon by reflecting a little on the comments that have just been made by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey). [English]
I think, Mr. Speaker, I understand the sentiments that drove the hon. member to make the statement which he just made, that the matters of language policy and bilingualism, the use of the official languages, should be taken out of the political arena, but if I may be allowed what I believe is an important distinction, I believe I would like to take a position slightly different from his. I do not think that a matter that is so vital to so many people in Canada can be taken out of the political arena. Of course, it stands to reason that we not only have the right but the duty to speak of these matters here in parliament, and outside of parliament as well.
Perhaps if he meant that matters of language and language policy should be taken out of partisan debate I would be more inclined to share his views, but the question is political, totally political. Our people are looking for a wise but nevertheless political answer. Of course, if it is going to be in the political arena we are going to hear strange noises from time to time. There will be extreme statements made by some persons. We are, after all, all of us human. There are 260 or more of us. I was going to say 260 odd, but sometimes that word is misunderstood. There are 22 million more throughout the country, and we all have freedom of speech as well as the responsibility that comes with freedom of speech. So it will be, when it comes to the language question, that you will hear jackasses braying on both sides. But perhaps we could take some comfort from the fact that a nation that brays together stays together.
I am simply putting it that way to underline the fact that all of us must feel free at any time to talk about these matters. If we, as representatives of the people, speak foolishly, then the people will take us to account. But in no way can we listen to exhortations that we stop talking about this matter in this parliament, in this country, and on the hustings. I, for one, have paid quite a bit of attention to this question. I was going to say for some ten years now, since the late right hon. prime minister Pearson said that there would be a commission on biculturalism and bilingualism, but my concern goes back further than that. As a matter of fact, if I remember correctly, the first time that the problem of language in this country struck me
Official Languages
was that morning in the early summer, or spring, I forget exactly when the date was, over 23 years ago when the Korean war was declared. If I may be allowed I will take some time to repeat the anecdote because it certainly had an influence on me.

At that time, I was working in a factory in the eastern part of Quebec City. The other workers and I used to gather in a square at 7:30 a.m. while waiting for the bus that would take us to the factory. Normally, while waiting for the bus, we would get together and chat.
Of course, the news of the day can be discussed, as well as all kinds of other subjects. At any rate, we were talking, chatting away as serious as you please, but that particular morning I was seated, reading a newspaper, the Journal de Montreal, dealing with the declaration of war in Korea. After a while, I noticed that I alone was reading and that my colleagues were grouped a little to the side. Three of them left the group and approached me, like a delegation. The oldest of the three said: "Listen, is there going to be war?" I replied: "I don't know, you see, I am just reading the newspaper, I don't know much about that". But he added: "If there was a war, would there be a draft?" Again, I replied: "I have no idea. Why ask me that?" They replied: "First of all, you go to college, and besides you are English." Mr. Speaker, I remembered that remark later on. That showed me, first of all, that class distinctions do exist in this country. We can set that matter aside, but let us speak of the second part of the question. It struck me and I have never been able to forget it. With all the good will in the world, one cannot help but notice that there is a difference, and that some people, and for good reasons, feel left outside of certain things; they do not feel that they are part of the great movements in this country. In this case, workers, most of them in their forties, would come and ask a lad of 17 what was going to happen because they thought that little guy knew, just because he spoke English. That struck me, and since then I have been interested in the problem of languages in my country. I certainly intend to discuss the matter in a political arena, and especially this one.
Mr. Speaker, it is a very complex matter, of course, and I have said nothing when I said that. We all know that. There are an enormous number of distinctions that have to be made and made by all of the members of this House with regard to the terms that we use to discuss language policy. Obviously, one major distinction is that an official language policy is not a bilingualism policy. Let us make that absolutely clear. You could have, for example, the complete, adequate and thorough operation of the Official Languages Act in the federal service and still have done very little toward the development of bilingualism, as such, across the nation.
Bilingualism has to do with a person being bilingual, with a person being able to speak at least two languages. That is why, Mr. Speaker, although I find it illuminating to some degree, I find it even more confusing to hear the language used very often around this House, around this hill and in the reports of the Commissioner of Official

May 17, 1973
Official Languages
Languages-the language which says that what we are after is institutional bilingualism. Mr. Speaker, institutions do not speak; people speak. I think that is a tremendously important distinction to keep in mind. The official languages policy is not the same thing as a bilingual policy. A bilingual policy does not mean necessarily a policy wherein persons who have only one language, who are unilingual, can have full rights. Obviously, we can see that the government is beginning to move toward this kind of distinction as it proposes the nine principles for our consideration. There is beginning to be a refinement of those distinctions; certainly, there is more refinement now than ten years ago when the "Bi-Bi" commission was first launched.
The speaker from the Social Credit party certainly made some very important points. I cannot agree with what he was specifying as a solution, perhaps because I have not thought about it fully.

But I find it rather difficult to understand him. Perhaps he will be able to explain to me, if we stay here long enough, what he means by a parallel government or a parallel system of government? It is not the story about Mr. Ryan-that I know very well-but when he speaks about duplication of services, I have some difficulty in understanding exactly what that means, and I ask him to be patient, not for a generation, but for sometime, because my colleagues have to study his suggestions. In a way, I come closer to his position, when I note the figures mentioned lately by the Official Language Commissioner, concerning the number of bilingual employees in the public service, because I realize that I must act soon, and vigorously. All hon. members may not have seen those statistics, but here is an excerpt of his text. I will quote that text in English, in order not to mispronounce the figures. Here they are:

Total public service appointments 1971 and 1972, distribution by language requirements: Bilingual 1971, 9.1 per cent; 1972, 7.6 per cent; French, 8.3 per cent in 1971, 11 per cent in 1972; English, 79.2 per cent in 1971, 75.6 per cent in 1972. The figures speak for themselves and they do not need to be underlined. I am sure they have been cited enough in this House to point out that whatever our good intentions may be, we are not moving fast in the direction of giving equality of opportunity to the French speaking citizens of this country. When it comes to service being provided to them by the public service of Canada, we certainly come nowhere near equality of participation by French speaking citizens in this country in the public service of their country.
It might strike a lot of people, Mr. Speaker, that the imposition of quotas is not a matter of common sense, that in the normal way of thinking that we have in this country we believe that people who try for jobs should deserve those jobs; they should be qualified and they should have merit. This is called the merit principle. But I should like to give this House a little warning about common sense. There are many things that we do, and that we believe, which are not common sense. For example, in a very important way it is not evident common sense that such a thing as a trade union movement is good. Obviously,

people who work harder should be allowed to move fast and earn more money. Why do we need an institution such as a trade union movement? We need such an institution, we have finally come to realize, because the common sense world we thought existed did not exist in the way we thought it did.
If you cannot follow the trade union example, let me give you another of what common sense tells us. For centuries, Mr. Speaker, all men and women said, "Of course, the sun goes around the earth; it is common sense, it is evident". They also said, "Of course, the earth is flat; it is common sense, we can all see it". So, common sense can be a very dangerous guide. What we, as parliamentarians, have to use very often is uncommon sense-a sense which takes us beyond the surface of things and makes us dig into patterns and shapes which control our lives and society.
So if I advance a notion, it is not exactly the same notion at all as the one presented by the speaker from the Social Credit party that there should be something like quotas for recruiting of personnel into the public service, I know I will be met with a barrage of remarks to the effect that it is not common sense. But I say that in order to preserve this country, and the solidarity of this country, we will just have to use more everyday common sense.
Mr. Speaker, I could give you many other examples of how we, in our society, have done things which at first glance do not stand up to casual, normal inspection, but we know that without those things and those institutions our society would not work.
I support the notion put forward by the speaker from the Social Credit party that we must concentrate on what he calls "participation"; that is the key to the solution of the problem. Eventually, how this participation is to be worked out will have to be a matter of considerable and thoughtful debate. Certainly, I support that approach. We have to make a collective decision about it and take collective action; otherwise, all we are talking about is motherhood and we are only involved in wishful thinking. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, I cannot identify with the monolingual Members of Parliament, whether English- or Frenchspeaking, because I can really say that I express myself fairly well in English and that I can also get by in French. I am in a rather fortunate position.
I thank hon. members for their applause, but there is no merit attached to such a position. I owe it to my mother, who is a French-Canadian. I did not learn French in school, although they tried to teach me a bit. But intellectually at least, I think I understand the position of the monolingual French-Canadian, especially in this House, because wherever he goes, he is aware that poeple think he is monolingual "for ulterior motives".
He must be aware that, although we are today discussing seriously the question of the official language in the public service, we are somewhat isolated in Ottawa, that the public service itself is somewhat isolated from the rest of the country, and that even if a completely bilingual public service could be achieved, that would not make it a bilingual country.
May 17, 1973

Just in case I am somewhat hard to understand because what I am saying is too abstract, I shall now give some concrete examples.
Here on Parliament Hill, everything is in English and in French: the signs, notices, paper work and translations. If you go out towards the fence around Parliament Hill, you see that the signs and notices are still bilingual, written in both the official languages. They say in French that it is "une impasse", and in English that it is one-way. So far so good, but as soon as you are outside this fence, this barrier, you find yourself in the real world of Canada, and the monolingual French-Canadian is confronted with a traffic light for pedestrians which says: "Walk-Don't walk'.
This is just an example, but I think it sums up the situation and that there are some alarming phenomena in this country. In the federal public service, some attempt is being made to introduce and encourage the use of both the official languages. You might say that we are encouraging bilingualism, but outside Parliament Hill and the public service, the trend is in the other direction.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote a few figures on the teaching of French as a second language in the Englishspeaking provinces and on the teaching of English as a second language in the province of Quebec.
