speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I will try to be brief. I think I can probably sum up in approximately three minutes; but may I point out that what I have to say in that time will in no way complete all I have to say on this subject.
I just want to make this one point. If you look at the figures having to do with the teaching of French in the English speaking provinces in Canada, you could be greatly alarmed. If you look at students in English speaking provinces across Canada who were studying French, I am speaking of students in high school, and express their number as a percentage of those who could study French, you will find that these figures hold true: In 1970-71, 55.7 per cent of the students who could study French, were studying French at some time during their high school career. I am not saying how much French they studied or for how long; I am merely saying that that percentage were exposed to some French instruction. In 1971-72, the percentage came down to 53.2 per cent. In 1972-73, the last year for which I have figures the percentage is reduced to 47.0 per cent. The decline is alarming, Mr. Speaker, and I predict that the figures for this year will be even more staggering.
I will end on this note: We cannot here discuss the matter of official languages, bilingualism and the rights of unilingual personnel in the Public Service, in isolation
Official Languages
from what exists in the rest of the country, because we could well discover ourselves moving in one direction while the country is moving in another. Although it may not be terribly relevant to the members of the Social Credit party if people in English Canada have some ability to speak French, it is terribly relevant to me, and to many others in English Canada. I, for one, want to ask the government to begin discussions with the provinces, with a view to reversing the present trend; otherwise, no matter what we do to improve the linguistic capabilities of our civil servants, we may well find that we have a bilingual civil service operating in a country that is essentially not bilingual, as may happen in a few years from now.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT TAKE MEASURES TO SAFEGUARD RIGHTS OF FRANCOPHONE AND ANGLOPHONE CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while listening earlier to the comments made by the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) in presenting his motion to the House I must say that at the very beginning I could not help smiling when, for instance, the hon. member thinking of the 15 seats won by his party in the province of Quebec did not hesitate to mistake those seats for the French Canadian population of Quebec.
I would remind the hon. member that population should not be counted in terms of seats but in terms of the individuals themselves and I think that the half million Quebec voters who have chosen the Progressive Conservative Party at the last election would feel quite uneasy in considering themselves among the official opposition as the hon. member for Champlain tried to recall.
I was also smiling because the hon. member for Champlain reminded me unintentionally of the comments made in this House by his leader on January 4 and 8 last, and I quote:
The differences of opinion with regard to linguistic matters did not constitute a real problem but that it was made to look like a problem because of a sad lack of purchasing power in all of the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, today the Creditiste party wants to plead in favour of bilingualism. It has the right to do so, even if people are concerned over extremely urgent problems. It has the right to do it because bilingualism is obviously of vital importance for Canada's future. But just the same we should be aware that the House will have to discuss this very problem within the next few weeks when it takes into consideration the resolution brought in by the government. And at that time an exhaustive study of the government plan already on the order paper will be undertaken.
In any event, opposition is our right here and we respect this right. With them, we shall officially reopen the very important record of bilingualism. I confess that I feel at ease to deal with the language policy in Canada in general and in the public service in particular. Just like several other hon. members of all political parties, especially the present leader of the government and the leader of the opposition, I can express myself adequately in both official languages of the country and I am proud of it.
On the other hand, since I have just mentioned it, I would like to add that I am particularly pleased to sit and to work at the side of the leader of my party; all hon.

May 17, 1973
Official Languages
members, like an increasing number of French-speaking Canadians, must recognize today the highly praisable and already very effective personal efforts he has been making for four years to speak correctly in French.

speechtext:
If the applause that comes from all sides is any indication, this is an eloquent and worthy example not only for parliamentarians as a whole but for all our fellow citizens. And this attitude, like the attitude of the other party leaders who are here, is worth many speeches and many votes of principle on bilingualism.
Mr. Speaker, all of us in this House, with more solidarity than ever, support the intent and direction of the lingustic policy sketched under the initiative of the late right hon. Lester B. Pearson and already launched in fact by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he was leader of the government.
It would be unfortunate if today, in an altogether regionalist spirit, a debate would harden even before it is formally restarted. Nobody will hasten the advent of a large concensus on a linguistic policy developed to its fullest by playing petty politics or harshly introducing a motion that would only deal superficially with the problem. If there is a legislative area where all regional barriers and especially political labels and narrow and partisan considerations must be put aside, it is indeed that of the official languages of a country. Without an open mind, without an unpolitical approach, without mutual understanding, we would easily become, some of us at least, overly racist. Since we have a mandate from our constituents, we have no right to be sceptics, even less pessimists; on the contrary, more than ever, we must stick together so that our flag, which proudly stands to your right, Mr. Speaker, will always be recognized and saluted by the two founding communities of our nation. Now, without any false modesty, I want to address all members in this House as well as all Canadians, and all those who will hear me, and tell them that as a Canadian and as a proud Canadian and French-speaking Quebecer; intolerance, never more! Mr. Speaker, I should also like to say that a new world is emerging in which the majority of Canadians are less than 35, in which the level of education and school attendance are unprecedented, in which the instruments of sub-culture such as the media and modern audio-visual aids develop creativeness as never before, in which people are more concerned than past generations ever were with world problems or with new disciplines such as cybernetics, environment and what not, and where especially, in this new world, dialogue and understanding take the form of community life.
New possibilities exist when interprovincial or international travels-and soon maybe interplanetary-take less than no time, waves know no boundaries, currencies move more and more freely, languages are easier to learn and allow you to discover other people and, finally, when modern pedagogy is both an animator and a catalyst of an international conscience. Finally, I would like to tell them, Mr. Speaker; we must find new solutions. Tomorrow it will be too late.
Are we, as parliamentarians or Canadians from British Columbia, the Prairies, Ontario, Quebec or the Maritimes,
[Mr. Wagner.l
again, out of ignorance, intolerance, selfishness, fear, or short-sighted political reasons, barely stated, to become responsible for or accessories to injustices vis-a-vis one or the other of the two founding groups, the two major linguistic communities of this country? Let those from the province of Quebec or elsewhere who cannot, can no longer or do not have to familiarize themselves with the other official language of this country from a practical point of view, allow at least their fellow citizens, let alone their children and grandchildren, to familiarize themselves with the other official language.
That is the way to build a Canada based on the sturdy, mutual respect of partnership.
On the other hand, let us not believe that national unity boils down to the sole question of official languages in this country.
Canada's two official languages, an easier access for French-speaking Canadians to the federal public service, federal services provided in both languages where necessary, even useful, of course, all that is part and parcel of our national unity theme. But basically and in our fellow citizens' every-day-life context, national unity will really be ensured at home by putting an end, in agreement with other levels of government and in a decentralization spirit, by putting an end to social and economic injustices and by tackling more effectively the problem of regional disparities in this country.
That is really our challenge as members of Parliament.
As far as the substance of the Creditiste proposal is concerned, it is only logical for me to think, in view of my earlier remarks, that it is clear: I intend to be more specific when the government motion is officially debated in the House. You see, Mr. Speaker, I am one of those who do not want, as we say, to put the cart before the horse, especially in this area.
In concluding, I wish to make it clear that the solution to the problem of bilingualism, though patterned on the proceedings in this House, will not be stem from the House. It is the whole country that must fall into step.
I think of the privileged class, the leaders, college students, academics' communication agents, publishers and other experts, professionals, leaders of social, cultural, economical movements, industrialists and businessmen, and when thinking of them all, I think particularly and first of all of those who live in Quebec and off Quebec. To all those I just mentioned, I say that the real solutions will come from them.
I want a Canada, Mr. Speaker, where Canadians choose to understand each other and communicate with one another. I want a Canada where the issue of language is not one of political gain but of coherent national leadership. Regardless of my own views as a politician, there are local and community opinion leaders who must do their fair share. The students, professionals, businessmen, farmers, fishermen and others who make up this land will have to make up their own minds and make their own personal commitment. I happen to believe that this commitment will be made. I happen to believe that those who underes-
May 17, 1973

timate this commitment underestimate Canada and Canadians; and what is more important Mr. Speaker, they underestimate themselves.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to learned speeches, I would like to tell the House, through you, that I also have a philosophical, a great speech on Canadian policies to make, but that I will not make it today.
I will not make it today for a very simple reason, namely that I am surprised-and I am not the only one-about the procedure adopted by our colleagues of the Social Credit party who deemed it necessary to introduce a motion on an opposition day, while since April 13th a resolution appears on the order paper in the name of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), by which the government announced its intention to allow everybody to take a stand on this matter of vital importance for Canada, which it considers as high priority. The House leader of our party (Mr. MacEachen) announced earlier today, early this afternoon, that this debate on the resolution put on the order paper on April 13th would take place sometime next week.
I will not take up extremely interesting views which have been expressed in several speeches made by previous speakers that I do not wish to take a position, because the government's view is that a debate in depth on this matter cannot take place today, since the motion introduced by the Social Credit party would not permit a beneficial fruitful and exhaustive debate.
I hasten to explain because I suppose our colleagues of the Social Credit party do not agree, but that is my opinion, that of the government, and 1 would like to specify the reasons for it. This motion does not permit a debate in depth on the matter, first because it contains wrong allegations about the Official Languages Act which is, of course, a major point in any discussion about official languages within the public service and, secondly, because it puts in a wrong light the debate that should be held on this matter, in stating views which we also consider as inaccurate. I will limit my remarks to try and establish those two points of view and explain by the same token our abstention from participating in this debate today.
I would like to show first of all that the first part of the resolution from the Social Credit Party set the debate on the wrong track even before it began. I quote:
That this House deplores the government's decision to postpone the full implementation of the policy contained in the Official Languages Act-
I should like to point out, through you, Mr. Speaker, particularly to the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) who spoke on this question and who is the sponsor of the motion that I think that assertion is incorrect, that the Official Languages Act can very well be implemented in the 60 months provided for in one of the last sections of the act, not in spite of but in the interest of the measures contained in the resolution of April 13 in

May 17, 1973
Official Languages
the name of the right hon. Prime Minister. As was clear at various points in his speech, the member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) apparently still entertains an extremely dangerous confusion, which has already been pointed out by some previous speakers, in connection with the official languages, personal bilingualism, and what, despite the objections of the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Harney), I shall continue to call institutional bilingualism.
Indeed, the member for Champlain made a case that seems to be based on a proposition that the government never formulated or defended. He seemed to be arguing against the idea that all federal civil servants, if not all Canadians, ought to become bilingual. There is a very strong expression in French, but I will use it all the same: the honourable member attributes this opinion to us, despite the fact that since the Official Languages Act was passed, we have been killing ourselves, killing ourselves I say, to explain that the bilingualism we are talking about in our policy on the official languages-I personally prefer the latter phrase-does not oblige every Canadian, or all federal civil servants, to learn two languages. It has but two aims. First: that all Canadian citizens be able to communicate with the Federal government and its related agencies in the official language of their choice, whether English or French; and, consequently, second: that if they work in the federal Public Service, they may also carry out their duties in-the official language of their choice.
It is therefore absolutely not a matter of forcing all Canadians to speakTboth languages, or even all civil servants. It does, however, mean that a certain number of civil servants, those who come into contact with the public or who hold supervisory positions and thus come into contact with junior public servants are bilingual, otherwise the two major objectives of the official languages policy could not be achieved.
Well, that is a policy, those are objectives the government has no intention to abandon, nor to postpone full implementation of measures which can be helpful in achieving them.
Second point: The Social Credit motion asserts that the government, in the resolution it tabled on April 13, proposes no efficient means of creating equality of the two languages within the public service, and that those measures proposed are neither realistic, nor concrete, nor fair, nor reasonable. I want to demonstrate the falsity of that premise which can lead only to equally false conclusions.
I shall demonstrate this as briefly as I can, Mr. Speaker, lest I get myself involved in a flagrant contradiction and, after having said that the substantial debate should not take place enter into such a substantial debate. However, I feel hon. members will recognize that, in order to point out the weakness of the Creditiste motion, I must show by contrast the strength of the resolution on the order paper.
Returning just one moment to the Official Languages Act, I was surprised by the kind of absolution whereby the hon. member for Champlain asserted that no progress had been achieved.
I feel that at leisure, when he thinks over his speech while going to sleep tonight-if it happens that he thinks over his speeches when going to sleep-he will realize that

he has exaggerated. I would like to give him a specific example. Now to suggest as he did that no progress has been made is an undefensible argument and I would like to give him a rather personal example. During the Holy Week both of us were in Cape Kennedy giving our moral support to the launching of a satellite-that was all we could do-and personally I was impressed-I am sure that the hon. member was too-to see that in a foreign country in Cape Kennedy, the officials who accompanied us and the employees of Telesat Canada were giving explanations to laymen such as we, some of which of a highly technical nature, in English as well as in French. I honestly ask the hon. member-and it is only an example-if we could only imagine five years ago that in a technical, scientific area- and this in the United States, in the heat of Florida-some people speak French because a certain number of the members of the parliamentary delegation spoke French.
I should not want to suggest for one moment that the hon. member is wrong to complain about the state of services in French in the Federal government because being part of this government, I find reasons to complain myself-perhaps not each day but nearly every week-and to try to correct these mistakes. But between this and going to the other extreme which consists in saying that no progress has been made, I think there is a gap which the hon. member did not see fit to consider and I hope that, in the basic debate that will take place when the resolution under the name of the right hon. Prime Minister will be discussed in this House, we will all try to stay within the limits of what is reasonable-I do not say of common sense but of what is reasonable-which is something quite different-and try not to go beyond our thought. We are in an area where emotion plays a great part and where it is unfortunately too easy to go beyond one's thought and to take extreme positions, which are indefensible for all practical purposes.
The hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) spoke about the difficulties which persist and which are real, I agree. Again, if I did not want to say it myself, I would just have to refer hon. members to the report of the Commissioner of Official Languages; these difficulties still exist and they are very real. I should say however to the hon. member that it is far easier to criticize them than to correct them efficiently and that in spite of the remarks he has made-and I personally found a great deal of factual truth in them-I am nearly as impatient as he is. I would like to tell him however that it would not be reasonable to indicate only the bad sides and to neglect completely the progress we have made.
Mr. Speaker, first of all, in dealing with the second part of the motion I would like to quote a few figures related to some of the progress we have achieved and which contradict the hon. member for Champlain who claims not only that we have stagnated but that we have even lost ground. We have lost ground in some areas, we do suffer from some stagnation, but there has also been some progress which I should like to review briefly.
First of all, I should like to advise the House that we have made progress in that the use of the French language is more widespread in the civil service. With regard to procurement, the Public Service Commission advised me that of the 88,000 appointments made in 1972, as compared
May 17, 1973

with 1971, there were 4 per cent fewer positions listing a knowledge of English as a compulsory requirement, while the number of positions requiring French increased by 3 per cent. I will admit that the progress is modest, but it is a fact. Of the 38,000 new employees recruited in 1972, 22 per cent preferred to work in French as compared with 19 per cent in 1971.
Disregarding the special recruiting of Francophones in
1971,	23.7 per cent of university graduates hired in 1971 were French-speaking, their percentage increasing to 28.3 per cent in 1972.
In 1972 also, French-speaking university students, administration trainees represented 33.5 per cent of all the trainees. At management level, the number of appointed Francophones has increased from 19 per cent in 1971 to 21 per cent in 1972. During that period, 41 per cent of all appointees in the management category were bilingual, compared to 34 per cent only in 1971.
As to training, the results are not as encouraging. During a five year period, the participation of Frenchspeaking employees in the centralized training courses given by the Public Service Commission only increased from 4 per cent to 9.5 per cent.
This is the reason why the resolution in the name of the Prime Minister provides for an increase of training courses available in French. At the beginning of 1972, 10.5 per cent of the Public Service Commission courses were given in French, and by the end of 1972, this percentage has been increased to 60 per cent. By the end of 1975, all Public Service Commission courses will be available in both languages.
However, in the important career assignment program which is intended for junior officers, the French participation increased from 12 per cent in 1969 to 30 per cent in
1972.
I could go on quoting figures but not, as I said before, in an effort to prove that the problem has been solved, because this would be absolutely ridiculous. A problem which has been aggravated for over a century can certainly not be solved in four and a half, five or six years. But, as one of our colleagues was saying the other day in this House, we should not take another century to solve it.
In my opinion, the rate of progress has been accelerating. We shall have considerations to make in this connection. I hope that the hon. member for Champlain himself, when the resolution comes before the House, will be more specific and will not complacently indulge in the same kind of vague proposals as those he has presented today but will explain the contents of today's motion and produce evidence that the measures provided for in our resolution are neither realistic, practical, fair, or reasonable.
I might say-but again I would enter upon the substance of the debate-that those measures are realistic when they provide, for instance, that anyone in a supervising position must be bilingual; I think this is extremely realistic. How is it possible for employees to work in English or in French if they are supervised by someone who is unable to read the memos they write or to understand the language they speak?
I would also like to say that these measures are practical by giving one example: the chance for French-speaking as
Official Languages
well as English-speaking people of learning the second language. French-speaking people also experience the need for a second language.
I think the measures are fair and that anything that looks like concessions in these measures is in fact aimed at protecting the rights of unilingual people to positions they have held for years. For instance, anyone who has been involved in union negotiations is aware of the fact that the safeguard of any rights acquired by a worker is something sacred with which nobody wants to tamper, even if at times these might appear as excessive concessions.
Finally, I think that those measures are reasonable and this is evidenced by the fact that the wording of this resolution has been fully approved by all the Public Service unions. Not only did they accept and approved the conditions stipulated and the measures provided in the resolution but they allowed us to mention this approval publicly.
I will stop at that, Mr. Speaker, and sum it up. We will take no further part in this debate, except perhaps to point out a few things and add a few remarks, because we believe that a truly substantive debate cannot take place until the resolution dated April 13 is introduced in the House for debate.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after the excellent speech delivered by my colleague, I feel it is important to point out the suggestions and statements made in another study on bilingualism, that of Dr. P. C. Coulombe. The surprising thing about it is that this one was conducted on behalf of the Treasury Board, but, as in most cases, it has been put away on the shelves.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) introduced his motion on bilingualism, did he take this report into consideration? You can pass judgment on it when considering the statements made in this study and the government's action. First of all, let us come back to the Treasury Board. In an article in Le Devoir of October 18, 1972, this was said, and I quote:
The bilingualism programs are inefficient and inadequate.
The report indicated clearly, with supporting data, that bilingualism too often consists merely in giving simple language courses which are, in addition, pitifully inefficient. From 1966 to 1971, those courses cost $54 million, and of the 22,807 civil servants who registered for them, only 1,851, that is 8 per cent, completed the program.
Attempts were made to silence the Francophones by creating French language units, but there again the results were deplorable. Those units included 2,497 civil servants in Ottawa, that is barely 5 per cent of the total work force in the public service.

May 17, 1973
Official Languages
What is even more deplorable is the fact that by sub-stracting the number of employees working in the Language Bureau, only 564 civil servants remain in the French Language units, that is 1.1 per cent of the total. Is that representation adequate? I do not think so. One does not have to be a genius to realize the seriousness of the failure. Even in Quebec, the system does not work. Only 55 per cent of the 44,000 federal civil servants in Quebec are grouped in the French units. Does that prove that the French language is respected in the civil service?
Instead of truly encouraging bilingualism according to the original intention of the government, the departments take unfair advantage of the translation services. That enables them to restrict the use of French. Why encourage the hiring of Francophones? They simply insist on translation and so employ English unilingual high officials who have their texts translated to make people believe that all goes well in the best of worlds.
You have there, Mr. Chairman, the hypocritical attitude of the present government as regards bilingualism.
The Coulombe report even indicates that the bilingualism goals set by the Trudeau government for 1975 will not be attained, far from it. Bilingualism in Canada, as advocated by the present government, is all poppycock. And we have sufficient proof of that.
Are people aware that it costs $29,000 to train a bilingual public servant and that it cost $54 million to train the 1,851 public servants who completed the course? Those are the figures.
From 1966 to 1970, the $17 million spent for the training of bilingual public servants may be considered as a total loss since 6,463 of those who had registered dropped out. Out of the 18,627 English-speaking public servants who registered, only 946, namely 5 per cent, completed the course. It was a real success, was it not? On the other hand, out of 4,090 Francophones who had registered, 905 met the course requirements, namely 22 per cent. That is not much better!
Apart from such a poor result, the appointing of higher officers always favours unilingual English-speaking people. Yes! We find those gentlemen in the upper levels and preferably where they are not in touch with the public. Such are the arguments in the Coulombe report. That is another conclusion that proves that my colleague, the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte), is right, but we shall get back to the matter later on.
Out of the 142 higher officers appointed from outside the public service between 1966 and 1971, only 27 were Frenchspeaking, namely 19 per cent, while the French-speaking people account for 30 per cent of Canada's total population. As regard the higher officers appointed from within the public service, that is by way of promotion, only 16 per cent were French-speaking, namely 42 out of 269. The worst part of it is that instead of improving conditions are deteriorating.
In 1967-68, the employment percentage as regards French-speaking people was 26 per cent; in 1970-71, it fell to 13 per cent, namely a 50 per cent decrease. The leader of

the official opposition and his predecessor would say that our system is good.
I said earlier that to silence the French-speaking people, French language units had been created but even in this case the established standards were not respected and that instead of favouring the unilingual French positions, as stipulated in the Official Languages Act, more and more bilingual positions are created within those units. Thus, it is possible to get around the standards and always at the expense of French-speaking people.
The study made by Dr. Coulombe for the Treasury Board is precise, detailed and unequivocal. The only conclusion we can draw from it is that the bilingual policy is a total failure in Canada. However not being satisfied with its failure, the government through the Prime Minister wants to confirm this state of affairs by presenting a motion concerning the unfortunate facts known to date. This motion even says that if a bilingual position is occupied by a unilingual individual, this individual can attend bilingual courses or request his transfer out however if he so desires, he may retain his position as after 10 years in the Public Service he is considered, as actually bilingual although he is not. What about that?
I am sure the Progressive Conservative members must be laughing in their sleeves at the reading of such a motion. But let us consider now the recommendations of this report. First, let me state the substance of this report. Here is what Dr. Coulombe says:
We are deeply convinced that true bilingualism in the Public Service implies that French should occupy a major position as an actual working language.
This is another tribute to the hon. member for Champlain who declared the willingness of the French-speaking people to participate truly in the Federal administration. Whether one speaks French with ease or not matters very little. What is important is to allow unilingual French Canadians to have access to the same rights of decisions and the same levels of administration as the Anglophones.
First the report of the Treasury Board clearly recommends that the French units be reoriented and reorganized. This sounds very much like the parallel administrations advocated by our group, the Social Credit Party.
It recommends as well that the number and the importance of these units be increased, particularly in the national capital and in more departments.
Does the government choose such alternatives? Not at all, Mr. Speaker. They put this report on the shelf and they continue to increase their failure. The report finally recommends exactly what the Social Credit Party has been requiring for a long time, namely French-speaking departments. It is essential that French-speaking public servants have the same career opportunities as their English-speaking colleagues and, to achieve this objective, only parallel administrations of French-speaking departments will give hope to French-speaking people.
Mr. Speaker, we are no longer speaking of bilingualism among people, but of bilingualism within the administration. Does that not mean respect for language rights in Canada? Every citizen has the right to communicate with
May 17, 1973

its government in any of the two official languages. Instead of paying $29,000 to teach a second language to a person who will retire within a few years, we want to establish a permanent bilingual system, while respecting the individual's ability, his skills of administrator, engineer, technician, expert in any field, without hampering it for language reasons. Being a good engineer has little to do with language, but rather with the knowledge of engineering. Therefore, I may be a very good French-speaking statistical expert with no knowledge of the English language and because I do not speak English, I am not entitled to the opportunities that the public service offers. I will not be allowed to get the necessary promotion to successfully end my career. This is a strange and backward attitude.
My ability depends on my skills, my knowledge of statistics and not on my language. At the same time, an English-speaking person with the same skills as I, a statistician with similar qualifications, and this is the situation which now prevails, would be entitled to reach the higher levels of management, not because he is a better statistical expert, but only because he can speak English.
Indeed such is the conclusion of the Coulombe report; it is also the finding of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism.
All studies, all statistics prove unequivocally that until now the government deprives itself of a certain expertise because Mr. or Mrs. So-and-So is not bilingual or unilingual and English-speaking.
Therefore, I repeat that bilingualism is not designed for individuals, but rather for the system, the administration. It is evident that a bilingual individual increases the cultural value of a country, but still it is not the responsibility of the government to force or compel the individual to speak two languages. However, the government must be able to answer individuals, to communicate with them in both official languages, French or English.
Consequently, the suggestion of the Social Credit Party of Canada to create parallel administrations is the only one capable of ensuring respect for the language rights of the public employees as well as of the population in general.
As it was so well expressed in the conclusion of the Coulombe report, French-speaking departments must be created to allow Francophones to take part in the administration in the same way as the Anglophones, to have access to the executive positions in the same manner as the Anglophones, without discrimination and, especially, with full respect for the rights of all citizens. You will note, Mr. Speaker, that such a system would ensure the permanence of bilingualism in the public service without, as things are now, swallowing up fabulous amounts in pure loss, because of the necessity of ever starting again and because of the drop out rate of public employees following bilingual courses.
Mr. Speaker, as the member for Temiscamingue, (Mr. Caouette), the leader of our party, said so well on other occasions, it is a fantasy to believe we can make a Frenchman out of an Englishman and vice versa. However, it is certainly possible to create institutions that will respect French- and English-speaking persons.
Official Languages
This is what the Social Credit is suggesting. This is a workable, realistic suggestion. Moreover it is beyond question today as we come to realize the enormous failure of the bilingual policy of the present government.
The evidence is overwhelmingly against the present system, facts speak for themselves, statistics corroborate and magnifying facts, and all this reflects the perspicacity of our party.
We represent French Canada and, in this capacity, we know that French-speaking people want to take part in the management of public affairs. Let us give them the opportunity to really show what they can do by adopting the only possible solution, that is the creation of parallel administrations in all the government activity areas.

Mr. Speaker, polite as usual, the members of the Social Credit Party stressed this afternoon that there were few members in the House to listen to them. Mr. Speaker, I do not think it fitting to speak at length, as it might be merely a preview of our debate in the near future, when the government introduces its proposal on bilingualism, but I would like perhaps to clarify one point, as it seems that our journalist friends are trying to confuse people, probably not intentionaly. At 6:30 this evening I listened to the CBC news, in which an eminent journalist gave a bulletin which, to my mind, misrepresented what is happening today in the House. It must be recognized, and I think it important to point out, that we are not debating a motion on bilingualism. We are debating an opposition motion proposed by the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte), which, to my mind, involves basically the same issues that we will be discussing in connection with the government proposal. For this reason I have tried to find motives, reasons or explanations for this motion, but, although I have listened attentively, I have been aware that the arguments put forward were more relevant to the motion we will be proposing than to the one before us this evening.
To return to the CBC news, it was claimed that we were debating a motion on which the French-speaking members were remaining silent.
I would like to take exception to that impression which was created by the CBC tonight and which is absolutely untrue, absolutely incomplete, not to say more. I think

May 17, 1973

that as French-speaking Canadians we would be happy to participate in this debate, but we think it would be useless to repeat the arguments we will be putting forward when the motion on bilingualism is considered next week. I would merely like to say a few words on a field which concerns me particularly since I happen to be Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State and bilingualism policies usually come under the jurisdiction of the department where I am fortunate enough to work with an exceptional minister. Mr. Speaker, I think that the impression which was created tonight by saying that bilingualism has not progressed is made up of absolutely unfounded assertions and statements which mislead people who wish to know all the facts. It is clear that bilingualism has not progressed with the pace anticipated. There is no doubt that the progress that we would have liked to see go a lot further have not reached the pace we would have hoped for but, Mr. Speaker, saying that all that has been done in the field of bilingualism is an absolute failure is a statement I am not prepared to accept and which, in addition, is not a true reflection of the situation.
Mr. Speaker, I think I can speak on behalf of the Department of the Secretary of State, a department which was set up by a minister whose reputation has been long established and who played an essential part, I think, in our desire to set up structures where French-speaking Canadians would not replace their English-speaking colleagues but would join with them to form a family truly representative of the two main founding elements of the Canadian nation.
Mr. Speaker, I will simply give you some figures leaving it to you and to the other members to draw the conclusion.
When we consider that in the Department of the Secretary of State, 16 per cent of the civil servants use French as their main language, that 14 per cent of them use English as their main language, but that 70 per cent of those who work for the Secretary of State are bilingual can we seriously maintain that that is not a substantial progress, an interesting achievement? That is enough to make me forget what little Latin I may have.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is time to tell the Canadian people that bilingualism has two aspects. We should not attach importance to one aspect only. The first is to teach the greatest possible number of people the use of both languages so that they can express themselves as much as possible and communicate so that a certain group of people can come to the national capital and work in their language within the federal agencies and answer people in the language of their choice, taking it for granted that there are of course two official languages. However, there is also another aspect, the aspect of the representation of French-speaking people and there I agree with my friends of the Social Credit when they insist on the importance of the representation of French-speaking people in Ottawa which must not be left aside and on the fact that we should not maintain the illusion that all problems will be solved in Ottawa once we have reached a sufficient degree of bilingualism.
But from the example of the Department of the Secretary of State, Mr. Speaker, I think that it is possible to make a continuing effort and to collaborate at all levels to achieve the basic objectives of a nation where the two

main groups can really play their parts not only in the field of the language but also through an effective, concrete and representative presence.
I listened this afternoon to the hon. member from Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) who with all the skill he is capable of tried to keep hon. members from taking a political stand on the policy of bilingualism. This is extremely clever, but I do not agree with his views.
I believe that if the political parties do not have the courage to take their responsibilities and as such to indicate clearly their views on the bilingualism policy, they do not deserve to govern the nation. And if individually, it is normal that hon. members give their views, it is also normal that parties, as entities representing an important component of the nation, give their opinion officially and definitely on the opportunity for changes that must be brought about, and on the necessity to adopt a bilingualism policy. And that policy must not be merely windowdressing which gives only the impression that, as Frenchspeaking people we are tolerated, but it must insure that we are going to play our part and that we are considered as equal partners.
I hope that each party will make it a point, through its members, to express its views officially and will not leave it to the French-speaking people to impose or to express their views on bilingualism. I will stay here to listen carefully to my colleagues to learn their views and get their advice, to hear them say if the member for Lapointe who is French-speaking is really accepted in Ottawa not merely in great words and statements but if in fact something will be done to bring about the necessary changes so that the Canada that we want to preserve can rest on firm foundations through the acceptation of the two main communities.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to end my comments by saying that I am confident in the light of the experience I have gained since 1968 and the progress often too slow which I have witnessed that we are mature enough to understand that the step we are going to take, we must take it together like men who realize that Canada's fate lies in our own hands. And it behooves us to be in the forefront, to prove by our policies and understanding between one another and toward the people that we are ready to make sacrifices on both sides, that we are willing to make decisions which will enable Canada to keep on playing the major role it has been playing throughout the world.
I feel that the meaning and the scope of the motion before us have not been explained to us by the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte). I believe nevertheless that he is wrong when he says that the official language policy has been postponed.
It is certain, however, that at a given time the quick rate of growth of some policies should be geared to reality and what should be sought is not to impose bilingualism through legislation, but rather to have members of the House and the people of Canada accept it. I feel that if each member plays his part and explains to the people what bilingualism is, what Canadians, whether French- or English-speaking want is really the same thing: the best Canada ever, where all citizens, of both founding people, can live in happy harmony, that goal will be really achievable.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to my colleague the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau) who discussed the duties of a Member of Parliament. He said it is the duty of parliament, of parliamentarians and of governments to lead and to explain so there can be understanding in our country as to what is meant by the Official Languages Act. Among the terms he used were "institutional bilingualism" and "personal bilingualism." I listened to him and agree with him. I say, with all respect to the hon. member, to the party he supports and to the government he supports that the failing with respect to bilingualism as a concept in Canada is not in the policy. The failing is that the government, which was charged with the basic responsibility of explaining that policy clearly and unequivocally to the people of Canada, did not do so in terms which they could understand. That is the great failing.
If ever there was a responsibility to be laid on a government and the head of a government, it was the great responsibility of the Trudeau government in this delicate and important matter to give an explanation to all Canadians so that my friend in the Creditiste party would not be debating with the hon. member for Lapointe and they would not be debating this matter with us. This government failed Canadians with respect to the understanding of that statute. That failing is their responsibility. Whatever has happened with regard to the misunderstanding since that time has grown out of that failure.
I represent a constituency from which many people come to work in the offices of the government every day. During the election campaign in my constituency I was faced with the failures of this government with regard to the implementation of bilingualism. I emphasize the word "implementation". During the election campaign I went from door to door and spoke to many thousands of public servants. Not one public servant said to me that he opposed the principles set forth in the Official Languages Act. That is to their everlasting credit.
We must remember the purpose of the Official Languages Act. It is to give equal status to two languages. The duty of all members of this House is to ensure that in the process of implementation there is equality and recognition of equity to all public servants. If we can solve the problems of public servants who are working during this period of transition, a period when we are trying to remake 105 years of history within a short period, we will have gone a long way toward fostering and promoting the spirit of the principles set forth in the Official Languages Act.
We are faced with the challenge of trying to rebuild and extend the spirit of 1967, the spirit of excitement and hope that characterized our centennial year. I say with some sadness that this government has succeeded in widening the divisions among Canadians to the point where it is difficult to see where any government, even one dedicated to disunity, could have done worse.
I wish to state what this policy of bilingualism means to me as a Canadian. Within the limits of practicability, Canadians should have the right to federal government
Official Languages
service in English or French. The public service should be attractive to English and French Canadians alike. Government officials should be encouraged to learn both languages in such a way that they never feel coerced. This should be so especially where it means that a public servant will be able to do his job better because of his knowledge. It does not mean that public servants, whether French- or English-speaking, should be penalized because they speak only one of our two official languages. The true spirit of bilingualism in Canada ought to be, and I am sure it will be, one of attitude and commitment to a certain perception of our society.
As a member of this House I would not like to see real bilingualism destroyed by a government that has become so preoccupied with mechanics and numbers that it forgets that in government buildings there are people who are very much concerned because they live in what I referred to on an earlier occasion as the eye of a bilingual hurricane. When we look at the problems of Canada, we look to the eye of that hurricane, the public service of Canada. We must not forget this very important principle.
In our search for equality, the feeling of equality and the commitment to equality we must not forget that entering into the public service and advancement within it must be based on equality of opportunity for all Canadians. The public service must be a place where Canadians can work together. In the time that I am here, I hope I will be able to ensure that the public service is a place where justice is not only done to every public servant but where justice is seen to be done as well.
I say to all members of this House that bilingual institutions have their own significance that sometimes goes unnoticed. Their presence is precisely a guarantee that the individual Canadian has a right to deal in his own language, with his own government. Bilingualism involves the right to be unilingual. That is my understanding. That right applies to both French- and English-speaking Canadians. The great misunderstanding that has arisen is that bilingualism in Canada has become equated with a form of coercion. That is what it means in some quarters. I am committed to the assurance that this will not occur and that this feeling will not continue.
Reference has been made to the bilingual resolutions which we will have an opportunity to debate in a few days. Those resolutions contain nine points. There ought to be a tenth point, namely, that "the proof of the pudding is in the eating." We can put all the fine sentiments on paper in both official languages, write books and paragraphs, make speeches in this House and elsewhere, do all the things expected of Canadians, make calls for unity, concern, understanding and compassion but they will not mean anything if those on the treasury benches, whether from the party that presently occupies that place, or this party that soon will, do not do their part to ensure that the real spirit of those fine words are honoured.
One of the major problems of the bilingual policy in the public service results from the government's failure to administer and administrate realistically. The cabinet has authorized more and more money for training in the public service, much more than $30 million. But the effectiveness of the program has been undermined. The government has failed to understand or accept the fact that the
26314-29J

May 17, 1973
Official Languages
language training program requires adjustments within the public service by the public servant. It has taken the government far too long to grasp the implications of the significantly low success rate and the high drop-out rate in language training. The government has mistakenly added language training to the workload of public servants without providing extra personnel. This has had a very serious effect at various levels in the public service which have spoken about it through their associations.
A survey of drop-outs established that at least two-thirds of the drop-outs had been forced to discontinue their training because it conflicted with their regular workload. It is true that many have complained about the unrealistic administrative policy of the government with respect to bilingualism. However, this must not be misconstrued-and I do not think the people I have talked to ought to be misconstrued-as being in opposition to the principles set forth in the statute.
We are pleased that the government has seen fit to establish, under the auspices of the Treasury Board, an extensive program to hire replacements for public servants assigned to intensive language training courses. The practice of pulling civil servants away from language training to take care of departmental duties has been costly and has weakened the program. Too many language students have failed to achieve any measure of competence, regardless of personal effort on their part, thus affecting their opportunities.
Leaving language training to attend to departmental matters, and then returning only to find one has fallen far behind, has discouraged too many eager people who want to learn a second language, whatever that language may be. The double-banking system which has been proposed to ensure that a position is covered when a civil servant is on language training may be an answer to this problem. It may well do away with the frustration and fatigue caused by the dual responsibilities of departmental duties on the one hand and language training on the other.
There is the question of advancement. I believe these language courses which some public servants can take and which others, at the moment, cannot take ought to be broadened so that all public servants, or at least those who want to attend language courses, have access to them. I believe there is still a lack of opportunity that many public servants find to be a great threat.
For example, there are approximately 55,000 women in the public service of Canada. About 15,000 of them are in the secretarial-stenographic group. Many of them are classified as ST-5s and if they are not bilingual they will probably remain ST-5s for the rest of their career. On the other hand, if they were capable of taking dictation in both official languages, they could move up to the ST-8 category. At this point they are not being permitted to take language training. Given this kind of irritation, it is no wonder that people are emotional about bilingualism in the public service, and the responsibility that rests upon the government, and indeed on this parliament, is a heavy one indeed. It is this government's failure, whether it likes to accept the responsibility or not.

The proof of the pudding with respect to the real spirit will be in the eating of that pudding. We have a long way to go in this country to restore, within the public service and elsewhere, the true meaning and the true understanding of what was meant when the statute was passed. I hope that with good will and understanding on all sides, by people in all parts of Canada, we will reach that objective. The responsibility for seeing that this is the case begins in this House of Commons with the government, which must ensure that that which has become the focal point of present difficulties, namely, the people who work within the public service of Canada, are given the proper atmosphere within which their talents can be utilized for the benefit of this country. In the name of those people, many of whom I have the honour to represent, I ask in the House tonight for that understanding.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT TAKE MEASURES TO SAFEGUARD RIGHTS OF FRANCOPHONE AND ANGLOPHONE CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my feeling that the motion we are dealing with tonight as presented by the Creditiste party is an irrelevant one. The motion urges the government "to find realistic and specific ways of safeguarding the rights of French and Englishspeaking Canadians in a much more just and reasonable manner". In fact, the government motion under item 34 on the order paper is designed to fulfill the aims of the Social Credit motion as it relates to injustice to French- and English-speaking Canadians.
On October 30 of last year the Liberal government discovered, that among other things, a large number of Canadians were indeed disturbed by the attempts of the Liberals to create an instant bilingual society in this country. Indeed, the great secrecy with which the Official Languages Act was being implemented, combined with injustices done in the name of bilingualism, created feelings of unease and resentment among many Englishspeaking civil servants, and this could not help but manifest itself in similar feelings on the part of English-speaking Canadian citizens throughout this country. This resentment stemmed not from any disagreement with the concept of Canada as a bilingual country but, rather, from the suspicion that the government was acting in an autocratic and prejudicial manner. For my own part, I think perhaps this had some basis in fact.
I agree with the Official Languages Act and that Canadians of the two major cultures should feel at home in their communications with their government. But the Official Languages Act is in no way a bilingual policy for Canada and the Canadian people. In many aspects of the civil service, ease of communication may exist in the predominant use of one language because certain occupations may not immediately require facility in both the official languages.
One of the major faults in the government's Official Languages Act is that the relevant policies were never adequately explained to the Canadian people. Somehow or other the people of Canada, perhaps by a method of osmosis, were supposed to presume what was the aim and the thrust of the government. Contrary to the members of the Liberal Party, who see this act as the great panacea for all Canadian bilingual aches and pains, I view it as relating to only one aspect of Canadian bilingualism.
What is the government trying to do to develop and to nurture a truly bilingual society, keeping in mind respect
May 17, 1973

for the other cultures that exist in Canada? May I for a moment talk about the creation of a bilingual country, a country that has respect for the two major cultures within its boundaries. While the federal government disburses large amounts of money to provincial departments of education for second language instruction, there is no stipulation, or no essential machinery set up to ensure that these funds are in fact used for these purposes. Consequently, in many provinces these funds are finding their way into school construction programs, salaries for other than second language staff, and so on. They are not being used for the purpose for which the federal government designed them. To create a bilingual Canada, surely we must start with young children. We have to start in the elementary schools and with pre-school education programs. Why is second language instruction not started by educational television before a child gets to school, and continued right through the early years?
The federal government ought to allocate funds for the proper training of teachers of the second language. Cultural exchange should be encouraged and expanded, especially exchanges between groups of young students. The federal government, in its disbursements to provincial governments for second language instruction, should attach strings, and such funds should be allocated for pre-school education as well as for in-school education.
Perspective must be used in viewing the proper role of the Canadian federal government in the attempt to create and maintain a bilingual society in our country. Bilingualism in Canada will not stand or fall on its implementation solely at the public service level. To simply create fluency in both languages would be to fall short of the ideal of bilingualism and biculturalism. Knowledge and understanding of sister cultures, with resulting new attitudes, will create respect for those cultures and cannot fail to lead to a united Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps from the early days of Confederation, French Canadians, particularly those of the province of Quebec, have had snow jobs performed on them and have been fooled by the so-called great bilingualism policies of the federal government. Experience has taught them, in the province of Quebec particularly, through successive elections at four-year intervals, to interpret election language and to reach the conclusion, after repeated disappointments, that bilingualism was actually a convenient parade sword to brandish exclusively during election campaigns, to be hastily returned to its sheath once victory had been achieved.
We listened a moment ago to the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau) who, by the way, is certainly not a worthy successor of his predecessor, Mr. Gilles Gregoire, who, when speaking of bilingualism, put forward striking arguments, quoted figures and spoke plainly.
When the hon. member for Lapointe referred to silent members, I had the feeling that he was speaking of members of his party, because as far as bilingualism is concerned, I have not often seen Liberal members get excited, except during election campaigns.
Official Languages
As regards Progressive Conservative members, it is quite unfortunate to realize it, but including their leader, they also consider bilingualism as a political asset in order to save face and try to save the last two ridings they still have in the province of Quebec.
I heard the hon. member for Lapointe say earlier that he was going to forget what little Latin he may have learned. I wonder why he refers to a third language, when we have such a hard time having a second one recognized.
Mr. Speaker, the House will have to take into account several factors in the implementation of this policy as well as in the development, if I may say so, of programs designed for the whole country. Hon. members from all across Canada have a tremendous responsibility to assume in this field. Perhaps they are less aware in western Canada, in the Maritimes or in Newfoundland of the social crisis existing in Quebec.
We must not hide the truth. In Quebec, at present, people think in increasing numbers, and it is much more serious. Often in the past people woke up too late. Hon. members should not do the same. Something is happening in Quebec and we must be blind not to see it, or still, we would have to hide our head in the sand. What happens then is that we get a big kick in the pants. I have a notion that many here are about to get one.
The Social Credit stand on bilingualism is a realistic one, and it will enable all Canadians from coast to coast to be heard and respected when dealing with the government. Of course, attitudes will be hard to change. In the exclusively English regions without any contact with French Canadians, problems of understanding and integration will persist, of course. In other words, many will find it hard to accept the French fact in Canada.
The Social Credit is recommending the establishment of parallel departments, so that when a French Canadian deals with a department, he will be sure to speak to a French Canadian. He will be sure to obtain an answer in French when phoning a department. He will be sure if he writes, to get an answer in French. He will not have to wait for three months to obtain a reply and the services of three translators will not be necessary. The French Canadians have been and still are considered as the poor relatives in the Public Service. This at least is shown not only in the findings of the Commissioner of Official Languages, Mr. Keith Spicer, before the House Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates on Tuesday April 10, 1973 but also in answers provided by the various departments, Crown corporations and other government organizations to the questions asked on January 17 last and which remained on the order paper until we obtained the answers yesterday.
Les us look at those answers signed by the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Reid). The questions asked were as follows:
Has the department, the agency or the board concerned adopted a definite policy on bilingualism?
And the second question read as follows:
What number and total percentage of that agency's employees are (a) English unilingual (b) French unilingual (c) bilingual?

May 17, 1973
Official Languages
Then, to check if progress had been made in the field of bilingualism the following question was asked:
In 1960, 1962, 1964, 1966 and 1970, what was the number and total percentage of employees of the same agency who were (a) English unilingual (b) French unilingual (c) bilingual?
Finally, to complete this information and to see what efforts the government was making to encourage bilingualism a last question was asked as follows:
By year since 1960, what was the total budget allocated for the development of bilingualism in that agency?
I will not talk about the stereotyped answer that we received on the first question: it was invariably that departments' policies on bilingualism are based on the requirements of the Official Languages Act, the Public Service Employment Act, the Translation Bureau Act and policies and directives prescribed by the government.
That answer, Mr. Speaker, does not teach us anything new. It simply confirms that if bilingualism does not progress or indeed progresses so little in the departments or government agencies it is on account of the policies and directives established by the government or as a result of the deficiencies of those policies and directives.
Mr. Speaker, I turn now to the answer given to the second series of questions: What number and percentage of employees of such and such a department or organization are French-speaking only, English-speaking only or bilingual? Some of the replies were suprising, as for example the following from the Department of Manpower and Immigration. The Department claims that its files do not contain this information, in other words that there is no way of knowing how many of its employees were Frenchspeaking only, English-speaking only or bilingual in 1968, 1969 and 1970; but the department adds that it received $11,000 in 1970, $174,000 in 1971 and $671,000 in 1972-73 for the development of bilingualism. It is amazing to learn that $976,000 has been spent to promote bilingualism, but that nobody knows how many unilingual or bilingual employees there are in this department.
The replies from the Department of National Health and Welfare are vague, imprecise. For example, this department and the Treasury Board Secretariat claim quite seriously that all non-bilingual employees are considered as unilingual, and that there is no way of telling how many are French-speaking only or English-speaking only. Finally, however, we learned that in 1973, for example, there were 6,559 unilingual employees, which is 91.2 per cent, and 565 bilingual employees, which is 7.9 per cent. This is typical of our findings in all government departments.
Mr. Speaker, the replies given by the various government departments and agencies on bilingualism indicate that contrary to what some people suggest, "French Power" is not a fact yet in Ottawa. Unilingual French-speaking people are a very small minority. In some departments and agencies there is not even one employee whose working language is French. French-speaking people must speak English to get a job in the Public Service, which is not the case for the majority of English-speaking public servants.
In conclusion, I would like to quote the remarks made by the Commissioner of Official Languages, Mr. Spicer,

before the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates on April 10 last. Mr. Spicer said, and I quote:
I would not wish to take more of your time with this introductory statement. But I believe I should recall what I have said many times, most recently in our second annual report: from our observation post, we definitely do not have the impression that the cause of bilingualism is advancing with giant steps. We sometimes hear that the French language and French Canadians are in the process of taking over the Public Service. However, the figures do not support these fears. On the contrary, the French language is still not getting a fair shake in the Public Service.
Mr. Speaker, Mr. Spicer said "still not getting a fair shake". He goes on to say:
Last year, I quoted rather discouraging figures on jobs filled in the public service in 1971, showing that it was then roughly ten times easier for a person speaking English than for a person speaking French to enter his country's service. The following new figures, even while reflecting a slight modification, will show you what I mean.
Here are the total number of appointments in the federal Public Service in 1971 and 1972 by language

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that when discussing such a serious matter, so important for good understanding among Canadians, one can hear stupidities like these which were heard a moment ago.
Mr. Speaker, it is also unfortunate to see that the present government, and those that preceded it, indulge, over the years, in endless talk of bilingualism. Now, we see the government backing away from the solution at the very time when all Canadians thought they could at last put their finger on the real solution to the serious problem of bilingualism in Canada. Unfortunately, we are disappointed, as all Canadians will be when they see that the government, in meaningless texts, do not produce the solution which we had been allowed to expect. The government is backing away from the problem. It is afraid of it. After having created a commission of inquiry for the purpose of defining a problem which was already known to us, it was not necessary to spend $10 million of public funds to learn what the Royal Commission of Inquiry on Bilingualism and Biculturalism taught us.
The commission, after extremely costly work, merely confirmed what most Canadians, and we in the House, already knew so well.
Mr. Speaker, on many occasions, the Creditistes have noted certain things, especially since 1962, and I, for one, when I first came to this House, found to my great surprise in a country which I thought was bilingual before 1962, that even in the House of Commons it was difficult to assert the rights of the French language. It was still more difficult than today, I admit it, at least as far as the House of Commons is concerned to command respect in our language, so that sometimes in the House, we were compelled to break the rules of that Canadian institution which should set the example in Canada. We found much to our surprise that our guide of parliamentary procedure was still only written in English.
After that, some Quebec politicians made fun of us. Others made silly remarks about our fight for the French fact in the House of Commons. Mr. Speaker, other members, for example, even Liberals, have congratulated us, on numerous occasions on our stand concerning bilingualism in Canada, not because we were narrow-minded, but because at the outset, we were surprised at the facts that existed in 1962.
Mr. Speaker, I could give many other examples of what happened in the House of Commons and outside. On many occasions, we have unfortunately found that the ministers statements are too often handed to us only in English, and I don't want to blame the ministers directly, because they receive statements prepared by departmental officers. A minister comes in the House and goes through the statement he has to make in a few minutes. At the same time, we also go through it. That is the main reason why we too often receive in English only statements that should be in both languages, in order to respect the bicultural character of the House of Commons and of Canada.
May 17, 1973

Mr. Speaker, there is also a situation that many hon. members find shocking. Even if some of us are familiar with the English language when, for instance, we phone certain departments, I would say that 95 per cent of the time, we are told-

"I am sorry, Sir. I am going to get you someone who can speak French."

And, Mr. Speaker, I have heard a lot of "Sorry, Sir" since 1962. We are in 1973 and these departmental officers give me over the phone the stock reply:

"I am sorry, Sir. I have been unable to find someone who can speak to you in French".
[ Translation]
And they have so much trouble finding someone able to answer in French that I am unfortunately obliged to wait often for five, six, seven or eight minutes before I can find someone in the department, when he is not gone on his coffee break, to give me an answer in my own language. And very often we do not have enough time to wait indefinitely for those honourable gentlemen of the public service and I might be accused of being impolite, but I often had to hang up in desperation.
Another subject supports very well the grievances that have been stated in this House since 1962. Let us say a word now about all the methods used in the different Departments. We had confirmation in this House, two years ago, that all bills were first drafted in English, as well as all administrative forms and that they were translated afterwards in French.
I do not have enough time to give proof of that tonight. But one has only to open the first three files on the desk of any member, which the member uses whenever problems crop up as to some electors, to find out that the forms were translated. As a matter of fact, they leave a definite after taste which shows that the original was drafted in English. I will give you an example-

Mr. Speaker, I could elaborate much longer on the way those forms are written and on the stupidity of the civil service which only gives the appearance of being bilingual because it is a "function of translation." There are no bilingual people in the Public Service. And in today's La Presse were quoted figures the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin) obtained yesterday in this House.
English unilingualism is faring well...
. . . 88.9 per cent in the Department of Environment, 65 percent in the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; 84 percent in the Department of Agriculture, 37.1 percent in Information Canada; 27 percent in the Public Service; 61.2 percent in the Treasury Board, 72.8 percent of the Secretariat of the Treasury Board; 61.4 percent in the Department of Urban Affairs; 48.1 in the Tax Review Board; 81.5 percent in the National Energy Board; 46 percent in the Canadian Radio and Television Council; 72.3 percent in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce; 28 percent in the Company of Young Canadians; 57.5 percent in the Tariff Board, 49.4 percent in the Canadian International Development Agency; 65.3 percent in Statistics Canada.
Those figures demonstrate exactly the opposite of what the Progressive Conservative party tried to have the people of Canada believe during the last election campaign when it was claimed, for instance, that a "French Power" had been set up in Ottawa and that the federal government was under its control. Now, Mr. Speaker, when we read articles in La Presse entitled "L'unilin-guisme anglophone se porte bien", (English unilingualism is faring well), which give statistics supplied by the public service, which itself is involved, we cannot doubt those statistics on public service unilingualism.
Mr. Speaker, during the last election campaign, the Progressive Conservative party tried to sell the false slogan of a "French Power" in Ottawa, and I am not obliged to repeat what I have already said time and time again, that is, that the Progressive Conservative party is the most anti-French Canadian party we have ever known since confederation.
Mr. Speaker, had that party been so pro-French Canadian, had it been so much in favour of bilingualism in the public service, today they could do better than the Liberals who are now in office and they could at least have given us a heritage as far as bilingualism in Canada is concerned, a heritage that we do not have today and that we are all seeking.
Mr. Speaker, it is with regret that we must still talk, after 100 years, of the so-called bilingualism in Canada, which should no longer be a problem, particularly in the public service and must ensure that bilingualism in Canada is fully respected and that everyone, as the hon. members for Champlain and Drummond (Messrs. Matte and Boisvert) said, be he a French Canadian or an English Canadian, can communicate with federal departments and agencies in his own language. Mr. Speaker, as far as the grievances we had to air in the House are concerned, we should not be called anti-English; we are pro-Canadian, we want the implementation of bilingualism in Canada and we want the Canadian people to be no longer laughed at by being fed wrong solutions or hopes that federal legislation will never make possible.
