rise and say a few words. X wondered why a party which I have always felt identified with national unity in the best possible sense, the Social Credit party, should have found it imperative and necessary to use this particular day to debate this very sensitive subject, when they knew full well that within a week or two they would have ample opportunity to discuss it more fully. At that time they could make a case that all parties could duly endorse, because this is really an all-party position on official languages, and they could do it in the most non-partisan manner, at the same time having full rein of the privileges of the House of Commons to make their case known across the country.
It is very perplexing to know why we have been subjected to this type of diatribe for most of the day. That is the best way to describe what has been the content of the speeches of the Social Credit party. I know of no one in that party who is more concerned about the case of bilingualism than I am, the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) and others who grew up in the minority in the province of Quebec, who understand what fair play is, who have never had to suffer economically or in any other way because they come from a minority position in la belle province.
I came here in 1962, Mr. Speaker, and I have seen the progress made since then. For the Social Credit party to suddenly take a negative attitude-and they speak for a large number of the people of Quebec in many important ridings-to give the impression which permeated every speech they made today, that there has been absolutely no progress in the case of bilingualism and the exercise of the rights of French-speaking Canadians in this country, in Ottawa, in the national capital, in the House of Commons, in the government and in the opposition, is to misrepresent the progress that has been made. It may have been slow, but nevertheless it has been made in good faith because of the co-operation of all parties over the last ten years since I was elected to the House of Commons and since the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) was elected.
To pretend that no progress has been made is a deliberate misrepresentation of the facts, and the hon. member knows that. I am perplexed and do not understand precisely what is behind this deliberate attempt to jump the gun on what will be a very important debate in this House of Commons in the next week or two.
One thing was said tonight, and it could very well have been a slip of the tongue; I do not know. An hon. member from the Ottawa area said, quite properly, that if the Official Languages Act was supported by the government and only the government, then we on this side of the House are guilty of not having explained it properly to Canadians across this country. But I was under the impression that this act was adopted unanimously by all parties in the House, and therefore all parties are obligated to explain that piece of legislation.
The first person I would turn to as an example of one who accepted that responsibility is the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) who, although not one of the younger members of the House, has painstakingly day

after day taken the trouble to learn the other official language of this country because he wanted to do so. His progress is there for all of us to measure. It is an example to hon. members on both sides of the House as to what can be done if we approach the language problem in the proper spirit. If he can do this, surely public servants can do it, if that is the price of progress and promotion in certain sensitive areas of the public service.
To skirt that fact is to play politics with an issue that could very well tear apart the very fabric of this country at a time when the average Canadian finally has accepted the reality that this is a bilingual and multicultural country and that every person has the right to be serviced, when dealing with the government, in either of the official languages. It is the responsibility of the public service to make sure that Canadian citizens are given that service in their own official language. This principle applies no matter whether we are talking about correspondence, oral communication or any other means of communication at our disposal.
We cannot run away from that fact after years of tortuous progress, after the courageous policy brought in and enunciated by the late Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson and adopted in this House after inspiring speeches by the then leader of the opposition, by the then leader of the NDP and by the leader of the Social Credit party, who has had the courage to stand up in the most nationalistic areas of Quebec and endorse bilingualism as a logical and realistic step for the future. If he had been here tonight and had listened to some of the silly speeches made by members of his party in his absence, I wonder what he would think. He would be ashamed of some statements which have been made to the effect that no progress has been made in ten years, because if that is so then all efforts throughout the past and in other cultural areas by people of various parties have been for nothing.
There is not enough time between now and ten o'clock to list the progress which has been made as a result of the efforts of the Social Credit party from 1962 onward. As I remember, it was the Social Credit party that raised the unfair position of French Canadians in our Crown corporations. People were saying that you could not find a single French Canadian capable of sitting on the boards of directors of our national railway.
That issue was raised by the Social Credit party. The chief spokesman was a Social Credit member, Gilles Gre-goire. I have not forgotten that debate. Today, many Canadians whose mother tongue happens to be French head Crown corporations. One heads Air Canada, another the CBC, and others play prominent roles in other Crown corporations. I am thinking also of departments such as the UIC, Supply and Services and many other similar departments. They are headed by Canadians who happen to be French-speaking Canadians in the same way as I am a Canadian who happens to be English-speaking.
We have got over this problem. As I have said before, in another decade we will get over the concept of hyphenated Canadians because our youngsters are more enlightened than we are, thank goodness. They understand that bilingualism is a mark of culture, understanding and education and that you are richer if you can speak two or more languages. There is hardly anyone of my generation on
May 17, 1973

both sides of the House who does not say, "I wish I were fluent in the other language."
Learning another language is like learning music. It is not easy. We have to be tolerant and understanding of the civil servant who cannot learn another language and finds his progress blocked. That is why hon. members must look at the resolution that was placed on the order paper in April. They will find that ample opportunity is now given for the unilingual civil servant who has been in the civil service for a number of years to apply for a bilingual position so long as he says, "I am prepared to learn the other language and I am prepared to accept the assistance of someone who is bilingual."
Certainly, if we cannot accept the nine points enunciated on the order paper, this country will not be together very long. This applies to everybody here. I think we all support the resolution. That is why I think the members of the Social Credit party are doing this issue a disservice by rising in their seats today and advancing the pretext that absolutely no progress has been made in the public service here in Ottawa. That is false. Everybody in that corner knows that I am just as much a Canadian, just as much a Quebecker, just as bilingual and just as dedicated to the concept of bilingualism as the hon. gentleman who just sat down, and I am political enough to recognize political expediency. It is wrong to say that no progress has been made under the Liberal government, because that is not the fact.
May I call it ten o'clock?

Mr. Speaker, I should like to participate, even for a few minutes, in this debate so as to tell my colleagues, especially those who are presently on the government side, that today they have put this House to shame by sneaking away under the pretext that a so-called debate has been delayed for over a month. subtopic: HOUSING-ROCHDALE COLLEGE-REPORT ORDERED BY ONTARIO ATTORNEY GENERAL ON ACTIVITIES-ACTION BY MINISTER OF JUSTICE
HOUSING-ROCHDALE COLLEGE-REPORT ORDERED BY ONTARIO ATTORNEY GENERAL ON ACTIVITIES-ACTION BY MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the record will show that over the past two and a half years I have urged the government repeatedly to tell this House why it has not been able to foreclose on the delinquent Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation mortgage on Rochdale College, Toronto. Two years ago I spoke on this topic during the adjournment proceedings. At that time the mortgage on Rochdale was $340,000 in arrears; today it is more than $800,000 in arrears. This is scandalous. On that occasion I was answered by the then parliamentary secretary to the minister of labour. He said there were social as well as financial considerations involved in the Rochdale affair and that on the positive side the government would have to consider the role that Rochdale plays with respect to the youth of Toronto and the surrounding area. That was very interesting. While I am not pressing this case because of its moral implications alone, I would like to give the House some background on the actual role that Rochdale plays in the Toronto area.
First, the Toronto police, the Toronto council, the town council of Mississauga and the Peel county coroner have called for the closing of Rochdale. It has been labelled a festering abscess in the side of Toronto, and Peel county coroner Dr. Martin Dobkin said that it was probably the largest drug distribution centre in North America. Fugitives from justice seek and find refuge in Rochdale. When the police attempt to make an arrest with a legal warrant, they are set upon by the hooligans who make Rochdale their home.
26314-30J

May 17, 1973
Adjournment Debate
Over the years that Rochdale has been in existence under the patronage of the federal government, many deaths have occurred in the college, most of them connected with the use of drugs. These deaths range from murder to suicide to accidental death. Most of them involve boys and girls in their teens. Young girls are lured to the college, influenced to take drugs and then kept there for the pleasure of the hoodlums, drug pushers and other social misfits. Some youths who have lived for a while in Rochdale have been described by doctors as human vegetables.
Only a few days ago yet another youth fell to his death from an upper floor window at Rochdale. Later, someone went into his room and threw a box of burning garbage out of the window. The box fell on a six-year old girl playing in the street. She is in the Toronto Hospital for Sick Children, in serious condition.
The school boards in the Toronto area have amassed evidence that the drugs which find their way into the schools can be traced to Rochdale; that is then the source. This year alone there have been more than 1,000 arrests of people in the Rochdale building or seen leaving the building. Some of these people are wanted criminals, but the vast majority are charged with drug offences. When this is multiplied by the five or six years the college has been in existence it can be seen that it is a situation that cannot be allowed to continue.
There is another scandalous aspect of this sordid story. That is the fact that the federal government is pouring thousands of dollars per year into Rochdale in Opportunities for Youth and Local Initiative Program grants. This allows the college to survive and to carry on its out-and-out war on society. The people of Canada are paying for this. It is a crime.
Rochdale and the city of Toronto are presently locked in battle over whether the so-called college should pay nearly $750,000 in back taxes. I say to the members of this House who represent Toronto ridings that their constituents are being blackmailed by the federal government. The federal government's refusal to foreclose and recover the property, and their policy of supporting the college with OFY and LIP grants, is helping the hooligans who run Rochdale to avoid meeting their responsibilities.
Earlier this year, Mr. J. A. Houston, Ontario regional director of CMHC, told the Mississauga town council that CMHC was powerless to foreclose the Rochdale mortgage. This is strange indeed in light of charges made this week by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) who charged CMHC with being too hasty in foreclosing mortgages. He cited the example of a constituent who had been forced to sell his home to avoid foreclosure by CMHC because of arrears in mortgage payments amounting to $358. On the one hand CMHC cannot collect hundreds of thousands of dollars from a rats' nest like Rochdale, but it can quite easily force the sale of a private home to collect $358. It could be that the homeowner in question was unfortunate enough to be a responsible, law-abiding Canadian citizen.
If there is something in the National Housing Act that prevents CMHC from collecting arrears or foreclosing on institutions like Rochdale, then we had better have a close look at the National Housing Act while amending legisla-

tion is before the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. I cannot recall any such provisions in the government's amendment, and if it is true that CMHC is powerless to take action on the Rochdale mortgage let us consider this deficiency in the law at an early opportunity. This is public money, and I cannot stand by any longer and watch it being used as though it belongs to CMHC or to the government. This government scorns parliament, but none the less it is responsible to parliament. We have a right to know all the answers in the Rochdale affair and in similar institutions such as Ottawa's Pestalozzi College.
Some time ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that scandals like the Watergate affair cannot happen in Canada. I do not believe it, Mr. Speaker. This Rochdale affair is beginning to smell more and more like a mini-Watergate and it is time the government told us what is going on.

speakeroldname: Mr. Norman A. Cafik (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: HOUSING-ROCHDALE COLLEGE-REPORT ORDERED BY ONTARIO ATTORNEY GENERAL ON ACTIVITIES-ACTION BY MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) has on several occasions expressed his profound concern, which I am sure is shared by all hon. members, about events which have taken place at Rochdale in Toronto. I want to make it perfectly clear that the federal government is prosecuting an action to gain control of Rochdale as fast as is legally possible. Indeed, the government began foreclosure action in August, 1971, and when CMHC was barred by the Supreme Court of Ontario from gaining possession of the building it was we, the federal government, who took the initiative of having an interim receiver appointed on behalf of all creditors.
I must say that anyone who suggests that the government is dragging its feet is displaying a disturbing ignorance of the facts of this matter. The interim receiver, appointed as a result of the federal initiative, has hired a large security force and has taken other extraordinary measures to police the building. We understand that the receiver will make an announcement relating to this matter tomorrow morning. In the meantime, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs wrote on April 13, over a month ago, to the metro Police Commission chairman and to the Attorney General of the province of Ontario setting out the federal position respecting Rochdale and offering full co-operation in the Attorney General's proposed investigation of that institution. With the consent of hon. members,
I wish to table copies of the minister's letter at this time.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I want to make it clear that it is the job of CMHC, the mortgagor in this instance, to provide accommodation for Canadians under the National Housing Act. This the corporation is doing to the best of its ability. It is the responsibility of the police to enforce the laws relating to drugs.
I want to reiterate that the federal government has done everything in its power to prosecute foreclosure. Our handicap is that we have had to live within the law. Surely, among ourselves as lawmakers we ought to understand what that is all about.
May 17, 1973

subtopic: MANPOWER-INTERNATIONAL NICKEL COMPANY- PROJECTED PRODUCTION AND EMPLOYMENT LEVELS- PROVISION OF INFORMATION TO DEPARTMENT
MANPOWER-INTERNATIONAL NICKEL COMPANY- PROJECTED PRODUCTION AND EMPLOYMENT LEVELS- PROVISION OF INFORMATION TO DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I asked the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) the following question, as reported at page 3370 of Hansard for April 17, 1973:
Has the minister obtained from International Nickel Company projected employment and production levels at this company over the next few years? If not, is it the minister's intention to ask INCO to provide his manpower consultative services with such information?
Subsequent to the question, the minister wrote me a letter in which he stated:
Like all the other private corporations, INCO is not required to make public information regarding its internal operations so long as it satisfies the requirements of any applicable provincial labour legislation.
This is a weak-kneed response from a government whose experience with boom and bust mining operations ought to have taught them something. The kind of reply the minister sent me flies in the face of any modern strategy of economic development. To illustrate, the Sudbury area planning study, carried out by the ministry of treasury, economics and intergovernmental affairs, dated March 1973, clearly states on page 9:
Actual growth will be determined by birth and death rates, migration patterns and particularly by economic factors affecting employment opportunities. In an economy dominated by two large employers, the plans of these two corporations are the largest factors determining employment opportunities.
It further states:
If substantial industry other than mining is established in the region, further additional population growth could be expected but the available evidence does not suggest such an assumption.
Our communities have to plan our development. INCO dominates our work scene and represents a great deal of public investment vis-a-vis deferred taxes totalling $238 million, no tax paid in 1971, tax holidays on new mines, depletion allowances, fast write-offs on equipment, municipal tax assessments on buildings only, population abatement grants, training on-the-job grants, manpower retraining grants and preferred freight rates to ship out our ore, and it is insulting to my constituents that we should be put into the position of having to ask about this company's plans. This company should automatically file its plans with the government and the community. The minister and this government have the colossal gall to say that this company's future plans are a matter of private concern.
It may be that this minister thinks this multinational corporation has been very sensitive and responsive to the dependence of the community upon it. But maybe the minister does not realize that INCO has as much concern for the people of the Sudbury basin as a tom cat has for a marriage licence. For example, the number of hourly-rated employees at INCO in July, 1971, stood at 18,224, and as of April 30, 1973 it was 13,487. This is a drop of 5,000 jobs at INCO in less than two years. In addition, some 2,000 salaried employees have been cut back in the same period.
Adjournment Debate
In addition to the jobs lost, our workers have paid often with their lives and more often with their health. Our environment has been devastated; air, water, vegetation and wildlife have shared a common fate as a result of noxious pollutants being spilled into the area. Our resources are being shipped out of the country. Neither the Ontario Tory government, the Liberal federal government, their buddy INCO nor other commercial interests have moved to create or entice secondary industry to provide for the future of the Sudbury basin.
Even now this government should instruct the CNR immediately to cut its freight rates in and out of northern Ontario as a first step in establishing a climate for economic development. This government's disregard for the residents of northern Ontario is matched only by the Ontario government's equally callous disregard, and is certainly in contrast to the many favours showered on the mining companies in whose back pockets they have found their pot of gold.
We of northern Ontario demand that INCO and other mining companies be compelled to sit down with government and labour and plan together an orderly development of our resources. We call on the federal government and the provincial government, with local input, to develop an economic strategy which will remove forever our complete dependence on the mining industry.

speechtext:
However, industrial specialists and manpower consultants of the department undertake on a continuing basis short and longer term industrial sector studies. This is accomplished through a variety of liaison activities, associations, unions and other government departments and agencies both federal and provincial. In this way the department keeps informed of technological changes, market shifts and other trends in industry, labour, education, and so on, which may affect the efficient operation of the labour market.
Employment and production level projections of any company, including the International Nickel Company, are matters which the company may or may not wish to publicize. However, as the minister indicated to the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) in a letter of April 18, departmental officers enjoy a good working relationship with INCO, as indeed with corporations in all industrial sectors. We encourage employers to inform us as early as possible of any decisions that will cause significant employment shifts, expansions and dislocations. Moreover, close liaison with companies such as INCO enables the department to keep abreast of all developments touching on manpower matters.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has spoken of colossal gall. It seems to me the colossal gall is on his part, because he is suggesting that the constitution of Canada should be disregarded. What colossal gall that is, and for him to

May 17, 1973

interject during my speech makes that all the more evident. Perhaps the hon. member is not aware that labour relations in this industry fall under the provincial government, and if not, as a member of this parliament he should be aware of this fact. Perhaps he is not aware of the fact that unions find it very convenient to have full corporate disclosure for use in their negotiating proceedings.
I do not know whether or not the hon. member is carrying a brief for any particular body tonight in suggesting that information which would be useful to unions in negotiations should be made available, but it is not the practice of this government, and it is not permissible under the constitution of Canada to make such information about the industries of the country available. subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-REQUEST THAT FAMILY ALLOWANCE PAYMENTS BE TIED TO COST OF LIVING INDEX PENDING INCREASES
SOCIAL SECURITY-REQUEST THAT FAMILY ALLOWANCE PAYMENTS BE TIED TO COST OF LIVING INDEX PENDING INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question I am debating tonight is very basic and deals with what I think is a normal and fundamental suggestion to the government, which if put into effect would tend to relieve the suffering of many hundreds of thousands of children of lower income families across the country until the government is prepared to implement the new family allowances benefits which they say will or should be afforded to Canadians in January, 1974.
My question was simply whether the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) would table an order in council to tie present family allowance payments to the cost of living index using January, 1973, as the base month to ensure that families receive some improvement in benefits starting at once, and retroactively instead of having to wait until next year. The answer from the Prime Minister was, to my mind, immature, irresponsible and unworthy of a person who leads this country. I have been asking questions on family allowances ever since the white paper on income security came out in 1970, and I have been asking them in a manner which I think has been reasonable.
Since the beginning of the session I have asked the minister responsible, and the Prime Minister, in a responsible way, if they would implement the family allowance bill immediately, because I feel that it would help families with small children who cannot fend for themselves and would relieve the ever increasing calamity of malnutrition and high cost of living. All I get is an irresponsible answer that if it had not been for the opposition, the family allowance bill would have been passed in the last session of parliament.
What have we accomplished in three years, Mr. Speaker? All we have is a new paper-but this time the colour is

orange-telling the people of Canada that the government has a new approach to family allowances but that it cannot be produced until later in the year. The minister responsible for the original family income security plan was convinced in the last session that his bill-after changing it once during the session-was the best thing for Canadian children. A bill was produced that brought nightmares to those high-priced bureaucrats who were charged with implementing the bill, which in turn would have brought worse than nightmares to the mothers of the country, who would have received the benefits, because of the administrative details which it contained.
Here we are, almost three years later, with a government that is incapable of controlling the disease of runaway inflation, with an incapability of controlling the runaway cost of foods, shelter and clothing, but with a complete and utter lack of concern to implement federal increases in a bill which would relieve the inability of the low and no-income families to partially meet the needs of their children. The present family allowances bill could very easily have been amended as it presently exists, if there was any semblance of sincerity by the minister, instead of playing political football with poverty-stricken Canadians.
All they would really have to do, if they were concerned, would be to amend the clause in the present family allowance bill, which signifies the amount now received, by a greater amount. The only other clause required would be the insertion of a clause dealing with annual increases in the cost of living. This was done very simply under the old age security bill and the war veterans allowances bill, and it could have been passed in record time. But instead the minister plays footsie with the provinces at conferences, and to get every ounce of press value bamboozles the Canadian public and the press, those creative gentlemen who profess to know what is best for the country.
I could state almost word for word what the answer to my question will be. It will refer to the great master plan that exists. But regardless of what I hear, let it ever rest on the conscience of the government that they have already failed miserably to help the children of our country, that segment of our society which we should be preparing, as it is our duty to do, to become healthy citizens of Canada in later years. It is a national disgrace that the government has shown its apparent inefficiency to meet the problem that exists.

He is really suggesting something that is diametrically opposed to everything that I thought his party stood for in the past, that is, legislation by order in council. How stupid can you get to suggest this?

I do know, by virtue of this motion. The hon. member is really suggesting that we change the law by order in council. That is impossible. It cannot be done
May 17, 1973

within the law affecting family allowances to bring down an order in council which would, in effect, change the amount to be paid in relationship to the cost of living or any other factor. I thought the hon. member would have known that before he asked the question.
Second, I thought he would have consulted his colleagues who seem to spend so much time in committees and elsewhere opposing actions through orders in council or dollar estimates, or whatever, to supposedly frustrate parliament. Surely parliament is the place where one should deal with this question, not through order in council.
The hon. member talks about us playing footsie with the provinces. Surely it is not too much to expect a federal Member of Parliament to realize that we live in a federal system and that we have a federal government and provincial governments. We have proposed to the provinces a new family allowance program which would offer benefits up to $20 a month per child. At the moment it is $7.21. That particular proposal carries with it the caveat that the provinces have the right, and indeed the obligation, to choose their own provincial priorities and they can adjust that amount depending on age or other factors which they think are relevant to the children in their province.
